design_detail: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis with meta-regression (PROSPERO CRD42021267812) of controlled experimental studies in healthy adults aged 18 to 65 that gave a measured dose of caffeine and measured that night's sleep (mostly polysomnography, three studies with wrist actigraphy). 24 studies included, all controlled crossover designs; pooled mean differences against control for total sleep time, sleep onset latency, REM onset latency, wake after sleep onset, sleep efficiency and sleep stages; meta-regression on the amount and timing of the final caffeine dose; subjective sleep summarized narratively.
can_establish: The average change in objectively measured night-time sleep after caffeine taken earlier that day, compared with no caffeine or placebo, in healthy adults in controlled studies, and whether the loss of total sleep time grows with the amount of the last dose and its closeness to bedtime.
cannot_establish: Effects in people who drink caffeine daily at their usual intake without abstaining first, in adolescents, older adults or people with insomnia; whether tolerance to the sleep effects develops with daily use (only five multi-day studies); next-day consequences of the lost sleep (not measured); or precise safe timings, because the cut-off model uses only the final dose and defines safety as a non-significant difference.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). Included studies: small laboratory crossover studies of healthy volunteers (6 to 63 participants), mostly young men, several in athletes or in middle-aged adults (Table 2, pp. 5-6).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy adults 18 to 65; controlled experimental design; measured caffeine dose; a measured night-time sleep episode ending in the morning. Excluded: naps under 90 minutes, caffeine more than 18 hours before or after the start of sleep, no sleep measures (p. 2). English-language, peer-reviewed articles only (p. 2).
sample.demographics: Habitual intake mostly low to moderate (for example under 300 mg a day, or one to three drinks a day), with abstinence periods ranging from none to 48 hours or the whole study (Table 2).
sample.attrition: Not applicable; one study without a measure of variance was excluded from the quantitative synthesis (p. 3).
sample.selection_effects: Healthy, mostly male, low-to-moderate caffeine consumers who abstained before testing in a laboratory: people who drink caffeine daily at higher amounts may be less affected (tolerance), and people with poor sleep may be more affected; the authors name these limits (p. 11).

exposure.measurement: Caffeine given as a measured dose (capsules, coffee, tea or supplements) in each study.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: single or split oral doses from 100 to 1200 mg (or 1.1 to 8 mg per kg body weight), with the last dose from 0 to about 16 hours before bedtime; five studies gave caffeine on 4, 6, 9 or 14 consecutive days (Table 2; p. 3). Typical caffeine contents used for the authors' modelling: a cup of black tea 47 mg, a cup of coffee 107 mg, a serve of pre-workout supplement 217.5 mg (p. 3).
exposure.polysubstance: Additional interventions such as exercise were allowed only if the caffeine effect could be isolated (p. 2); smoking, alcohol, oral contraceptives and other factors affecting caffeine clearance were largely controlled within studies, according to the authors (p. 11).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Varied by study, from no abstinence to abstinence on the test day, for 48 hours or throughout (Table 2).

comparison.controls: The same participants without caffeine (placebo or no caffeine) in a crossover design.
comparison.matching: Within-person comparison; time in bed comparable between conditions in all but four studies (p. 8).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Genotype (CYP1A2, ADORA2A) and habitual intake were not accounted for in the included studies (p. 12).

outcomes.instruments: Polysomnography in most studies; wrist actigraphy in three; subjective sleep by sleep diaries, visual analogue scales and the Leeds Sleep Evaluation Questionnaire (Table 2).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors use clinical thresholds of 20 minutes for total sleep time and wake after sleep onset, 10 minutes for sleep onset latency and 5% for sleep efficiency (pp. 8-9).
outcomes.operationalization: Sleep disruption as less total sleep, longer sleep onset latency, more wake after sleep onset, lower sleep efficiency and shifts from deep to light sleep.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported at review level; polysomnography scoring blinding varies by study.

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects REML models with crossover correlation imputed from four studies (sensitivity analysis in a supplement), nested random effects and robust variance with small-sample correction (p. 3). Against control: total sleep time -45.3 min (95% CI -61.5 to -29.0), k = 37, n = 340; sleep onset latency +9.1 min (3.8 to 14.4), k = 32, n = 280; wake after sleep onset +11.8 min (2.5 to 21.0), k = 17, n = 148; sleep efficiency -7.0% (4.0 to 10.0 lower), k = 31, n = 274; REM onset latency -1.5 min (-8.1 to 5.2), not significant; N1 +6.1 min (2.3 to 9.9) and +1.7% (0.2 to 3.1); N3 plus N4 -11.4 min (printed CI -4.3 to -18.5) and -1.4%; N2 and REM unchanged (pp. 3-6, signs checked on the rendered pages). Meta-regression for total sleep time (k = 30, n = 262): timing p = 0.032 and amount p = 0.037; the loss was 2.8 min smaller (0.4 to 5.2) for each extra hour between the last dose and bedtime and 0.2 min larger (0.01 to 0.31) for each additional mg (p. 4). No heterogeneity statistics, prediction intervals or publication-bias tests are reported.
analysis.covariates: Meta-regression on the amount and timing of the final dose only (p. 3, p. 11).
analysis.selective_reporting: Subjective outcomes were not pooled because measures differed (p. 6); EEG spectral outcomes summarized narratively.
analysis.power: Not applicable; individual studies were small.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In healthy adults in laboratory crossover studies, caffeine cut that night's total sleep by about 45 minutes on average, lengthened the time to fall asleep by about 9 minutes, added about 12 minutes of waking during the night, lowered sleep efficiency by 7 percentage points and shifted sleep from deep to light stages. The loss of total sleep was larger with larger amounts and with caffeine taken closer to bedtime, but the other outcomes were not detectably moderated by amount or timing.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and practice points (pp. 1, 12) give cut-off times before bedtime for coffee and for pre-workout supplements and state that black tea can be drunk at any time; the cut-offs are the first time at which a model of the final dose crosses statistical significance, which the authors acknowledge assumes that significance equals clinical relevance (p. 11), and the black-tea statement treats a non-significant estimate as no effect. The values are not repeated on this card because the library gives no timing advice.

timeline.event: Clark and Landolt, systematic review of epidemiological studies and RCTs: caffeine associated with shorter, poorer sleep, without a quantitative synthesis (cited as ref. 21)
This meta-analysis: 16 of the 20 studies measuring total sleep time found a significant reduction (p. 8).
The same team's meta-analysis of alcohol and that night's sleep, with the same methods

replication.where_it_stands: The direction of the effect on total sleep time is consistent across most included studies and with the earlier qualitative review; the size of the effect at usual daily intake in habitual consumers, and the timing model, are less certain.

funding.funder: Not reported (no funding statement found in the article).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest (p. 12).
funding.affiliations_note: Australian Catholic University (SPRINT Research Centre), Leeds Beckett University and Central Queensland University; sports-science authors.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized crossover trial in habitual caffeine consumers at their usual intake, crossing several amounts with several times of the last dose, measuring sleep at home over weeks of daily use (to test tolerance) and next-day function, with genotype recorded.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items are not met (4, 7, 13 and 15), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2. The rating concerns how far the pooled numbers can be trusted as an unbiased summary: the included studies are mostly low risk of bias crossover experiments, the direction of the effect is consistent (16 of 20 studies for total sleep time), and the statistical methods are appropriate, but the search was narrow, publication bias was not examined, heterogeneity was not reported and the risk of bias of the studies was not used in interpretation. Cite it for the average effects on that night's sleep in healthy adults; do not cite its cut-off times.

key_findings.finding: 24 studies were included, all controlled crossover designs; five gave caffeine on several consecutive days. Risk of bias: 16 low, 3 some concerns (no randomized order) and 5 high (no washout, or sleep stages reported for part of the night only).

design_detail: Single-centre, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group randomized trial at the University of Basel anaesthesia department: 40 adults who regularly consumed a lot of caffeine and were having minor elective surgery under general anaesthesia, asked to stop all caffeine from the preoperative visit, randomized to caffeine tablets matched to their own usual daily intake (Group C, n = 20) or identical placebo tablets (Group P, n = 20). Outcome: headache and other possible caffeine-withdrawal symptoms on a standardized checklist before induction, on the evening of surgery and the next morning.
can_establish: Whether replacing the usual caffeine with tablets, compared with placebo, changes how many regular caffeine consumers report headache in the day after minor surgery, which in this randomized design isolates the part of postoperative headache that is due to going without caffeine.
cannot_establish: How often caffeine-withdrawal headache occurs outside a fasting, surgical setting (anaesthesia, surgery, opioids and fasting may add to or mask symptoms); effects on symptoms other than headache with any precision (counts of 0 to 10 per group); safety of the tablets beyond gastric volume and acidity in 40 people; and the claimed benefits on craving, fasting compliance or costs, which were not measured.

sample.recruitment: Clinic: patients scheduled for minor surgical procedures (plastic or reconstructive, orthopaedic upper or lower limb, gynaecological) with general anaesthesia at the University Hospital Basel, Switzerland; surgery between 8 and 10 a.m. Recruitment period and number screened not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: age 20 to 65 years; ASA class I or II; considerable daily caffeine intake (threshold on the card's exposure field); no history of frequent headaches (once a week or more); non-smokers; no current medical treatment; no surgery on the head or neck (p. 790, Methods, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Group C: age 47.2 (SD 16.8, range 22 to 61), 6 men and 14 women, weight 66.8 kg; Group P: age 48.4 (SD 19.6, range 18 to 55), 7 men and 13 women, weight 74.9 kg (Table I, p. 791). Mostly women (27 of 40).
sample.attrition: Not reported; tables show 20 per group at every assessment, implying no losses, but withdrawals or exclusions are not mentioned.
sample.selection_effects: Heavy caffeine consumers without frequent headaches, non-smokers in good health, having short morning operations: the findings describe people able to keep to strict caffeine abstinence in hospital, and may differ for people with migraine or chronic headache, smokers (who clear caffeine faster) or longer operations.

exposure.measurement: Usual caffeine intake estimated at the preoperative visit from an average weekday's consumption with published caffeine-content factors (p. 790). Abstinence and adherence checked by plasma caffeine (gas chromatography) during surgery and on the first postoperative day (Table IV, p. 791), reported only as group means.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: usual intake 430 mg a day (SD 143.6) in Group C and 380 mg (SD 168.9) in Group P (Table I); inclusion threshold at least 200 mg a day. Group C received oral caffeine tablets equal to the person's own average daily intake, half with the premedication (about one hour before surgery) and half at 3 p.m. on the day of surgery, and the dose was repeated at 7 a.m. on the first postoperative day (the text does not say whether the full or half amount was repeated). Group P received identical placebo tablets on the same schedule. Caffeine abstinence from the preoperative visit, about 16 to 18 hours before surgery (p. 790).
exposure.polysubstance: All patients received standardized anaesthesia: midazolam premedication, thiopentone, fentanyl and succinylcholine for induction, nitrous oxide and isoflurane, and paracetamol and/or methadone after surgery (p. 790). Analgesic totals did not differ between groups: paracetamol 1675 (SD 440) against 1450 (SD 470) mg, methadone 4.8 (SD 3.2) against 5.4 (SD 4.1) mg, caffeine group first (Table III). Smokers were excluded; alcohol not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Caffeine abstinence instructed from the preoperative visit; plasma caffeine in Group P 0.2 (SD 0.15) before surgery and 0 on day 1, against 2.2 (SD 1.8) and 2.9 (SD 2.3) in Group C (Table IV; unit printed as mg per ml, see reporting issues). The text states that no patient drank caffeinated drinks, based on these group values.

comparison.controls: Identical placebo tablets made by the hospital pharmacy, given by a ward nurse from blinded vials prepared by an anaesthetist not otherwise involved (p. 790).
comparison.matching: Randomization; groups similar in age, sex, weight, usual caffeine intake, type and duration of surgery and analgesic use (Tables I to III), with no formal tests reported beyond NS labels.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Headache history apart from the exclusion of frequent headache, migraine, anxiety, sleep the night before surgery and hours of fasting were not reported by group.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same anaesthetic and analgesic protocol in both groups; methadone and paracetamol totals similar (Table III).

outcomes.instruments: Standardized checklist administered by an anaesthetist who did not know the study drug: patients were asked explicitly whether they had headache, nausea, vomiting, fatigue or unsteadiness, and whether they had consumed caffeine (p. 790). Assessments immediately before induction, at about 6 p.m. on the day of surgery and on the morning of the first postoperative day (9 a.m. in Table V). Gastric fluid volume and pH from a gastric tube after intubation.
outcomes.validity_norms: Yes/no symptom questions; no severity rating, no validated headache scale.
outcomes.operationalization: Headache counted as present or absent at each visit; vomiting counted as more than two episodes.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Five symptoms at three times (15 counts) plus gastric volume and pH were compared at P < 0.05.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Patients, ward nurse and assessing anaesthetist blinded to allocation (p. 790). Patients who had been heavy caffeine consumers might notice withdrawal symptoms, but these are the outcome itself.

analysis.effect_sizes: Headache, placebo against caffeine: 10 of 20 against 0 of 20 at 6 p.m. on the day of surgery (P < 0.001) and 7 of 20 against 1 of 20 the next morning (P < 0.05) (Table V, p. 791). Editors' calculation (Newcombe score method): risk difference 50 percentage points (95% CI 24 to 70) on the evening and 30 points (95% CI 5 to 52) the next morning; Fisher's exact test p = 0.0004 and p = 0.044. Other symptoms did not differ significantly (for example nausea 4 against 7 on the evening and 0 against 4 the next morning). Gastric volume 19.2 (SD 14.6) against 22.7 (SD 11.9) ml and pH 2.12 (SD 1.63) against 1.91 (SD 1.24), both NS (Table IV).
analysis.covariates: None. The text reports no correlation between headache and age, sex, type or duration of surgery, without statistics.
analysis.preregistration_detail: 1995 trial; no protocol or registration mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All checklist symptoms are tabulated at all three times; no prespecified primary outcome is stated, though headache is the stated aim.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 40 regular heavy caffeine consumers kept off caffeine for minor surgery, half of those given placebo reported headache by the evening and about a third the next morning, against none and one of those given their usual caffeine as tablets. No other symptom differed detectably, and gastric volume and acidity were similar.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Discussion (pp. 789, 791-792) call the reduction highly significant and suggest that prophylactic caffeine tablets be considered for surgical patients used to a high intake; the Discussion adds that the tablets may reduce craving, improve compliance with fasting and reduce costs, none of which was measured, and argues from group-mean plasma levels that aspiration risk is not increased, which a trial of 40 people cannot show. The abstract says headaches persisted in seven patients until the next day, while Table V gives only counts at each visit.

timeline.event: Fennelly, Galletly and Purdie (Anesth Analg) link postoperative headache to usual caffeine intake in surgical outpatients (cited as ref. 6; not in the library's references).
Silverman et al. (N Engl J Med) describe a withdrawal syndrome after double-blind caffeine cessation in volunteers (cited as ref. 13; not in the library's references).
Weber, Ereth and Danielson (Mayo Clin Proc): caffeinated drinks after surgery reduced postoperative headache (cited as ref. 8; not in the library's references).
This trial: by the authors' account the first test of caffeine given prophylactically around surgery.

replication.where_it_stands: A single small trial. Within this paper it agrees with the cited volunteer and surgical-outpatient studies; no later replication was read for this card.

funding.affiliations_note: All authors from the Department of Anaesthesia, University of Basel/Kantonsspital; the tablets were made by the University of Basel pharmacy.

what_would_settle_it: A registered, adequately powered randomized trial of caffeine replacement around surgery in regular caffeine consumers, with a graded headache scale, sequence generation and concealment described, analysis by intention to treat, and safety outcomes (aspiration, nausea, heart rhythm) reported with intervals.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Blinding was well arranged and the outcome assessor was unaware of allocation, but sequence generation, attrition and a prespecified analysis are not reported, and the reporting errors listed below (an ineligible age in the placebo group, an impossible standard deviation, a wrong unit) lower confidence in the care of reporting. None of these would plausibly create a difference of 10 against 0 headaches. The trial may be cited for the size of the headache difference in this surgical setting; it should not be cited for safety or for symptoms other than headache.

design_detail: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD 42019120220) of blinded, placebo-controlled acute caffeine challenge studies in adults with clinician-diagnosed panic disorder, with or without psychiatrically healthy controls. 10 within-person studies (1985–2015; 8 with randomized order, 2 with caffeine always given last), 244 people with panic disorder and 122 controls, single oral challenge protocols (480 mg in 7 studies, 400 mg in 1, and 2 weight-based protocols; Table 1 labels one caffeine citrate, whose caffeine-versus-salt basis is unclear). Pooled outcomes: occurrence of panic attacks after caffeine in people with panic disorder versus controls (risk ratio, 6 studies) and self-rated anxiety change after caffeine (Hedges' g within each group and between groups, 6 studies). Placebo anxiety data were too sparse to pool, so the anxiety analyses are of change after caffeine alone.
can_establish: That selected blinded oral laboratory caffeine challenges at rest in medication-free adults with panic disorder were followed by panic attacks in about half, with none reported after placebo, and about 2% of healthy controls after caffeine; and that anxiety rose more in the panic-disorder groups on average, with substantial variation. These protocols do not establish a lower-dose threshold.
cannot_establish: Responses to ordinary smaller servings or a dose-response relationship; effects during psychotropic treatment or outside the laboratory; an exact caffeine-equivalent dose range for the citrate-labelled protocol without its primary report; the placebo-controlled magnitude of anxiety change; an exact pooled panic risk ratio(two incompatible versions); or mechanisms.

sample.recruitment: Searches of PubMed, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library to 14 October 2019, developed with a librarian, plus reference lists of included articles; English-language published original articles only, no date limit (Methods 2.3–2.4, pp. 23–24). Patients in the included studies were recruited from outpatient clinics in nine studies (not reported in one) (Results 3.2.2, p. 25).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: randomized placebo-controlled or controlled clinical trials in adults with panic disorder diagnosed by a clinician on DSM-III to DSM-5 or ICD-9/10 criteria; acute oral or intravenous caffeine against a placebo with identical or similar taste, given blind (double blinding and randomized order not required); anxiety on a continuous scale and/or panic attacks within 24 h; laboratory or clinical settings (Methods 2.2, p. 23). Excluded at full text: 3 without a placebo arm in a group, 2 without usable data, 1 without original data, 1 that told participants they were receiving caffeine, 1 with wrong outcomes (Results 3.1, p. 24). Studies of healthy people only were excluded, a disclosed deviation from the protocol (p. 23).
sample.demographics: Panic disorder groups of 7 to 83 people, mean ages 32.5 to 42 years (one study gives a range of 18–55), 50% to 79% women; control groups of 7 to 28, 36% to 73% women (Table 1, pp. 25–26).
sample.attrition: Within studies: 4 participants in two studies (Klein 3; Tancer 1), all from the caffeine condition (Results 3.7, p. 27). At review level: 18 full texts assessed, 8 excluded (p. 24).
sample.selection_effects: Small clinic samples tested off medication, at rest, in laboratories; English-language published reports only. The 10 studies come mainly from two research groups: four by Nardi and colleagues (refs 38–41) and four with Uhde among the authors (refs 34, 51, 53, 60), so they are not independent replications.

exposure.measurement: Investigators report giving caffeine/placebo blind in all studies(p.25), but Figure 2 rates participant/personnel blinding unclear in about 20%; the unread per-study supplement prevents resolving which feature was unclear.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: single oral challenges. Seven studies print 480 mg and one 400 mg; one protocol prints 7 mg/kg, and Charney prints caffeine citrate 10 mg/kg in ginger ale. The text converts the weight-based conditions at 75 kg to 525 and 750 mg of caffeine; the latter assumes a caffeine basis not clarified for the citrate-labelled preparation. No independent salt-to-base conversion or minimum tested caffeine amount is established here. Capsules in 2 studies, instant coffee in 5, other liquids in 3; rest afterwards and outcomes 30–240 minutes later.
exposure.polysubstance: All included challenge studies were done during abstinence from psychotropic treatment (Discussion 4.2, p. 28). Alcohol, nicotine and other drug use are not reported in the main text; duration of caffeine abstinence and fasting before testing were extracted (p. 24) but appear only in Table S2 (not read).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Caffeine abstinence before testing was extracted but is not reported in the main text (Table S2, not read).

comparison.controls: Within-person placebo sessions in all 10 studies; psychiatrically healthy controls given the same challenge in 7. The pooled contrasts are people with panic disorder versus controls after caffeine, and change after caffeine within each group; caffeine versus placebo is described only narratively for anxiety.
comparison.matching: Not described at review level; age and sex by group in Table 1.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Baseline anxiety sensitivity, respiratory subtype and ADORA2A genotype (examined in none of the included studies, p. 28); habitual caffeine use was extracted and said not to differ between groups (Table S2, not read; p. 28).

outcomes.instruments: Anxiety: visual analogue scales, Subjective Units of Distress, Spielberger State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (state), Zung Anxiety Scale and an NIMH rating, self- or clinician-rated, at 30 to 240 min; panic attacks: proportion with a self- or clinician-reported attack (Table 1, pp. 25–26). Pooling in R (metafor, meta, dmetar): Hedges' g with a random-effects model, correlation between baseline and post-caffeine anxiety imputed as 0.5 with sensitivity analyses from 0.1 to 0.9; risk ratios by Mantel-Haenszel (Methods 2.8–2.11, p. 24).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard anxiety scales; a panic attack is defined by each study (self- or clinician-reported). Risk of bias with a modified Cochrane tool by both authors (Methods 2.7, p. 24; Fig. 2, p. 26).
outcomes.operationalization: Panicogenic effect: panic attack after caffeine (none occurred after placebo). Anxiogenic effect: rise in anxiety from before to after caffeine, and its difference between people with panic disorder and controls.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Four primary pooled estimates (panic-attack risk ratio; anxiety change in each group; anxiety difference between groups), plus sensitivity analyses for the imputed correlation and time points (Table S3, not read).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level; study selection by both authors independently, extraction by one and checked by the other (pp. 24).

analysis.effect_sizes: Panic attacks after caffeine: 121 of 237 people with panic disorder (51.1%) in 9 studies and 2 of 115 controls (1.7%); none after placebo in any study (p. 27). In the 6 studies with both groups, 69 of 128 (53.9%) versus 2 of 115 (1.7%); log RR 3.47 (95% CI 2.06 to 4.87), Q(5) = 8.45, p = 0.133 (p. 27). Editors' calculation: this is RR 32 (7.8 to 130); it is reproduced exactly by a Mantel-Haenszel RR without continuity correction with the Greenland-Robins interval, whose denominator rests on the 2 events in one control group; the forest plot (Fig. 4, p. 27) instead shows RR 12.12 (6.06 to 24.23), prediction interval 3.78 to 38.83, I² 0%. Risk difference 52.2 percentage points (editors' calculation). In the 3 studies without controls, 52 of 109 (47.7%). Anxiety (6 studies, 121 with panic disorder, 111 controls): change after caffeine g 1.94 (1.19 to 2.69) in panic disorder and 0.91 (0.46 to 1.36) in controls; difference between groups g 1.02 (0.09 to 1.96), Q = 15.0, p = 0.01, I² 66.8% (20.7% to 86.1%) (p. 26); prediction interval −1.27 to 3.32 (Fig. 3, p. 27). Editors' recalculation from the forest-plot values: the Hartung-Knapp method with DerSimonian-Laird between-study variance reproduces 1.02 (0.08 to 1.96); without the study flagged as an outlier (Nardi 2009, g 2.51) it gives about 0.72 (0.07 to 1.37).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD 42019120220, registered 16 January 2019, updated 30 October 2019(search 14 October). Two deviations are explicitly described: mood dropped and healthy-only studies excluded. Methods also explain dose-response infeasibility and Results explain missing placebo-anxiety data; these are not undisclosed merely because not listed under the protocol-deviation heading. The registry was not read, so its full prespecification cannot be verified. The panic estimator is described inconsistently.
analysis.selective_reporting: Two different pooled risk ratios are printed (text and abstract versus Fig. 4) without explanation of which is the primary result. The prediction interval for the anxiety difference, which crosses zero, appears only in the figure. No sensitivity analysis without the funnel-plot outlier is reported.
analysis.power: Not assessed; the authors call the number of studies small and ask for replication in larger challenge studies (Limitations, p. 29).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 9 small laboratory studies, about half of 237 medication-free adults with panic disorder had a panic attack within hours of an oral challenge protocol (mostly 480 mg as printed; the citrate-labelled protocol has uncertain caffeine-equivalent basis), none was reported after placebo, and 2 of 115 healthy controls had one after caffeine (difference about 52 percentage points in the studies with both groups). Self-rated anxiety rose after caffeine in both groups, more in people with panic disorder on average, but this pooled difference (g 1.02) has a prediction interval from −1.27 to 3.32, shrinks to about 0.7 without one outlying study, and rests on change after caffeine without a placebo comparison.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that caffeine at doses roughly equal to 5 cups of coffee induces panic attacks in a large share of people with panic disorder and discriminates them from healthy adults, which the counts support; its pooled log RR (3.47) is one of two incompatible estimates in the paper. It also states that caffeine increases anxiety in patients and healthy adults at these doses (p. 22); the abstract's own limitations note that placebo anxiety data were lacking, and the discussion grades the anxiety effect as less certain (p. 28), but the within-group effects are uncontrolled pre–post changes. The statement that caffeine targets important mechanisms of panic disorder (p. 22) is not tested by the data. The clinical implication (inform patients, with the caveat that little is known below 480 mg) is appropriately qualified.

timeline.event: Charney et al.(1985): earliest included study; Table 1 prints 10 mg/kg caffeine citrate in 21 people with panic disorder/agoraphobia and 17 controls, caffeine always last. Whether the amount is expressed as caffeine or citrate is unclear; primary unread.
Nardi et al. (2007–2009): four included studies from one group, including the largest panic sample (83, no controls) and the outlying anxiety effect (g 2.51) (refs 38–41); not read.
Vilarim, Araujo and Nardi (2011): earlier systematic review of caffeine challenge in panic disorder without meta-analysis (ref 55); not read.
Masdrakis et al. (2015): latest included study, 400 mg instant coffee in 19 people with panic disorder (ref 59); not read.
This review: by the authors' account the first meta-analytic estimate of caffeine's panicogenic and anxiogenic effects in panic disorder against healthy adults.

replication.where_it_stands: The only meta-analysis of caffeine challenge in panic disorder on the reading lists. The panic finding is consistent across studies (all six point the same way); its size as a ratio is uncertain because almost no control had an attack, so the proportions are the better summary. The review does not establish effects of ordinary smaller servings or a precise lower tested caffeine dose because the citrate basis is unresolved. The included studies were not read for this card.

what_would_settle_it: A blinded, randomized dose-ranging challenge study (placebo and several doses including everyday amounts of 100 to 300 mg) in people with panic disorder and matched controls, with anxiety measured after placebo and caffeine on the same scales, repeated challenges to test reproducibility, and adequate samples of people on and off treatment.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population, acute caffeine challenge, placebo and healthy-control comparisons, anxiety and panic outcomes specified (pp. 23).

domains.domain: 2. Protocol registered before the review (critical)
domains.note: Registered on PROSPERO on 16 January 2019 (searches covered records to 14 October 2019), with two deviations disclosed and justified (p. 23); last updated on 30 October 2019, after the search date; registry not read; changes in the anxiety analysis and the panic estimator are not presented as deviations.

domains.domain: 3. Explanation of study designs included
domains.note: Blinded placebo-controlled challenge studies (RCTs and CCTs), with a reason for restricting group comparisons to studies that tested both groups (pp. 23–24).

domains.domain: 4. Comprehensive literature search (critical)
domains.note: Six databases, librarian-built strategy (examples of terms given) and reference lists; but English-language published original articles only, without a stated reason, no grey literature or registries, and searches more than two years before publication. Applied as written per senior decision 21 (2026-10-25).

domains.domain: 5. Study selection in duplicate
domains.note: Both authors screened independently in Covidence (p. 24).

domains.domain: 6. Data extraction in duplicate
domains.note: One author extracted and the other checked, disagreements resolved by discussion (p. 24); meets the consensus criterion as applied on sc_mcketin_2019.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Table S1 of the online appendix (Appendix A, p. 2) lists all 8 excluded full texts with the reason for each (read 12 November 2026).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives diagnosis, numbers, age, sex, caffeine vehicle, dose, order, anxiety measures and times, and panic counts; Table S2 of the appendix (p. 3) adds medication washout, caffeine abstinence, fasting and habitual caffeine use (given for 5 of 10 studies); the placebo vehicle is not given (appendix read 12 November 2026).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: A modified Cochrane tool covering sequence generation, concealment, blinding, incomplete data and selective reporting, by both authors (p. 24); suitable for the caffeine-placebo element, but the pooled contrasts (panic disorder versus controls; change after caffeine) are not randomized and confounding was not assessed. Per-study judgments in Fig. S3 of the appendix (p. 7, read 12 November 2026) match Fig. 2; Fig. 2 shows assessor blinding unclear in most studies.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

domains.domain: 11. Appropriate statistical methods for meta-analysis (critical)
domains.note: The panic estimator is described as random-effects Mantel-Haenszel in the Methods and fixed-effect in the Results, continuity correction is said both to have been and not to have been applied, and the text's pooled log RR (3.47) differs from the forest plot's RR (12.12) without explanation (pp. 24, 26–27). The anxiety effects of caffeine are pooled as uncontrolled pre–post changes, and the interval method is not stated.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis by risk of bias (for example excluding the two fixed-order studies).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The risk-of-bias results (Fig. 2) are not discussed anywhere; the limitations cover the small number of studies, the imputed correlation, inexact instant-coffee doses and reproducibility (p. 29), not the risk of bias of the included studies.

domains.domain: 14. Heterogeneity explained and discussed
domains.note: I² with its interval and prediction intervals reported; the heterogeneity of anxiety effects is discussed, with no study features found to explain it (pp. 26, 28).

domains.domain: 15. Publication bias investigated (critical)
domains.note: A close call: funnel plots for both outcomes, with one study flagged as unusually large for anxiety (p. 27); with 6 studies no test is possible, and the flagged study was not followed by a sensitivity analysis or a discussion of its impact.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding with funder role and a conflict declaration (pp. 29–30).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No longer provisional: the online appendix, read on 12 November 2026, settles item 7 (excluded studies listed with reasons, Table S1). Three critical items are not met (4: English-only published articles without justification; 11: incompatible pooled risk ratios and inconsistent model description; 13: risk of bias never discussed), which gives critically low confidence under the AMSTAR 2 rules. This is a judgment about the pooled numbers, not about the raw counts, which are transparent: Table 1 lets a reader see that about half of the people with panic disorder and almost no controls had a panic attack after caffeine, and that none was reported after placebo. Citable for: those proportions, the doses and conditions studied (selected oral protocols, mostly 480 mg as printed, at rest, off medication; the caffeine-citrate basis is unresolved). Not citable for: a precise risk ratio, a placebo-controlled size of the anxiety effect, effects of everyday caffeine intake, or mechanisms.

key_findings.finding: Searches of six databases to 14 October 2019 (English-language published articles) gave 2647 records; after removing 754 duplicates, 1893 were screened, 18 read in full and 10 included.

The Results say participants were blinded in all; Figure 2 rates participant/personnel blinding unclear in about 20%. Table 1 footnote 3 says one Tancer participant received caffeine only, so not every participant had both sessions. Overall 244 people with panic disorder and 122 healthy controls; 3 studies lacked healthy controls.

The text converts at 75 kg to 525 and 750 mg; the citrate protocol caffeine-versus-salt basis is unstated. Participants rested; outcomes 30–240 minutes later.

reporting_issues.issue: Two incompatible pooled risk ratios for panic attacks: the abstract and text give log RR 3.47 (95% CI 2.06 to 4.87) with Q(5) = 8.45, p = 0.133 (pp. 22, 27), while Fig. 4 (an image; values read from it) gives RR 12.12 (6.06 to 24.23) with χ²(5) = 1.58, P = .90 and I² 0%. The Methods describe a random-effects Mantel-Haenszel estimate computed without continuity correction (p. 24); the Results describe a fixed-effect Mantel-Haenszel analysis using continuity correction (pp. 26–27).
reporting_issues.consequence: Editors calculations reproduce the text as a fixed-effect Mantel-Haenszel estimate without continuity correction, depending on 2 control events in one study. Figure study ratios are approximately consistent with continuity correction, but the Charney row does not exactly reproduce from printed counts and the exact pooled figure method is not identifiable. Retain both printed estimates as an inconsistency; use counts for the descriptive comparison rather than silently choose or repair one.

reporting_issues.issue: Study counts by outcome disagree: Results 3.2.4 says nine studies measured anxiety and eight panic attacks (p. 25), but the synthesis and Table 1 show nine with panic data and eight with anxiety data; Results 3.5.1 says only 2 studies reported placebo anxiety data and, two paragraphs later, only 3 (p. 26).
reporting_issues.consequence: The counts appear swapped or miscounted; use Table 1 and the synthesis (9 panic, 8 anxiety).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives Klein et al. as 5/17 (71%) with panic attacks in a group of 7; 5 of 7 is 71%, and the total of 121 of 237 requires 7. The Masdrakis row labels its 19 participants as healthy controls although they are people with panic disorder, and a template placeholder (YY.Y) is left in the Charney row.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typesetting errors; the pooled counts are consistent with n = 7 for Klein and with Masdrakis being a panic disorder group.

reporting_issues.issue: The prediction interval for the difference in anxiety rise between panic disorder and controls (−1.27 to 3.32) appears only in Fig. 3 (an image; values read from it); neither the abstract nor the text mentions that it includes zero.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's statement of increased sensitivity to caffeine-induced anxiety in panic disorder is presented without the uncertainty shown in the figure; together with the outlier, this makes the anxiety comparison weaker than the abstract suggests.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods list six risk-of-bias domains (p. 24), but Fig. 2 shows seven (adding other sources of bias); the panic counts are referred to Fig. 2, which is the risk-of-bias figure (p. 27).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor cross-referencing errors.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 labels Charney’s intervention caffeine citrate 10 mg/kg, while the text converts it at 75 kg to 750 mg of caffeine without stating the dose basis.
reporting_issues.consequence: The caffeine-equivalent amount and the claimed 400–750 mg range require the primary paper. Do not assert a no-study-below 400 mg boundary or convert the salt label by assumption.

reporting_issues.issue: Results state participants were blinded in all studies, while Figure 2 rates participant/personnel blinding unclear in about 20%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Blinding was reported but not equally well documented; per-study supplement needed to resolve.

reporting_issues.issue: Tancer’s 90-minute STAI value is used in the pooled anxiety comparison, although a larger patient/control difference was reported only at 150 minutes on a different scale.
reporting_issues.consequence: This is a disclosed time-point choice, not proof of an effect at every assessment; alternate-scale sensitivity results are in the unread supplement.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 footnote 3 says one Tancer participant received only caffeine, qualifying the Results statement that all participants received both conditions.
reporting_issues.consequence: Keep the descriptive caffeine numerator/denominator distinct from an assumed complete paired placebo denominator; no 237-person placebo denominator inferred.

design_detail: Randomized, counterbalanced, open-label crossover trial in a free-living setting (University of Birmingham, UK). 52 healthy non-smoking men who habitually drank 3–6 cups of coffee a day were enrolled and 50 completed both arms: on three trial days (after a control day) they drank four 200 mL mugs of black instant coffee intended to provide 4 mg/kg body mass of caffeine a day (trial C) or four 200 mL mugs of water (trial W), with all food individually prescribed, provided and replicated in both trials, each man's daily fluid set from his diary and provided as bottled water (whether the test drinks counted within it is not stated), and alcohol and exercise other than walking prohibited; 10-day washout on their usual diet and caffeine. Outcomes: total body water by deuterium oxide dilution (days 1 and 3), nude body mass (days 1–3), two 24-h urine collections and three morning urine samples, and fasting blood on days 1–3.
can_establish: Whether, in caffeine-habituated healthy young men on a controlled diet, 800 mL a day of instant coffee (mean 308 mg caffeine) changed urine output, body water, body mass or blood and urine hydration markers over three days compared with the same volume of water.
cannot_establish: That coffee and water hydrate equally (no equivalence margin, no confidence intervals, no power calculation); anything about women, people who rarely consume caffeine, larger intakes, other coffee preparations or longer periods; whether caffeine or other coffee components are responsible (no decaffeinated arm); or the urine response in the first hours after each cup (only 24-h totals and morning samples were measured).

sample.recruitment: Volunteers; how they were recruited is not described. 52 men were accepted after screening of over 100 volunteers (Methods › Participants, p. 2); trials ran Tuesday to Friday, February to December, at a university sport-science laboratory (Methods › Study Design, p. 3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Men aged 18–46, non-smoking, weight stable, passing a general health questionnaire, free of medicines containing caffeine or affecting weight or fluid–electrolyte balance, living and working at stable ambient temperature, without extreme food, drink or supplement intakes, free of chronic illness, and drinking 3–6 cups of coffee a day (300–600 mg/day caffeine) by a 3-day weighed food diary; anyone whose caffeine from coffee fell outside 300–600 mg/day was not included. Women were excluded because of possible menstrual-cycle effects on fluid balance (pp. 2–4).
sample.demographics: Table 2 (p. 5): age 28.1 (SD 7.3, range 18–46) years; height 181.1 (SD 6.3) cm; weight 77.0 (SD 12.1, range 51.1–133.6) kg; habitual energy intake 2400 (SD 464) kcal; total water intake 2081 (SD 842, range 1083–3614; unit not printed); habitual coffee intake 979 (SD 301, range 625–1522) mL/day. Ethnicity and education not reported. Whether Table 2 describes the 52 enrolled or the 50 completers is not stated.
sample.attrition: 2 of 52 did not complete because personal circumstances prevented laboratory visits (p. 3); analyses use the 50 completers. Per-marker sample sizes (p. 4): urine volume and specific gravity 50, urine osmolality 46, urine creatinine 48, urine sodium 46, urine potassium 42; haematocrit 48, serum osmolality 49, total plasma protein 48, serum creatinine 46, serum sodium 45, serum potassium 45, attributed to missing samples or technical error. Total body water is shown for 25 participants (Figure 2, p. 5) with no reason given.
sample.selection_effects: A small, healthy, young, male, non-smoking sample of habitual moderate coffee drinkers from a sport-science volunteer pool, chosen to be habituated to caffeine (the introduction notes that regular consumption may lead to tolerance to caffeine's diuretic effect, p. 1). The results cannot be carried over to women, to people who rarely consume caffeine, to older or ill people, or to larger intakes.

exposure.measurement: Assigned intervention. Coffee: four pre-weighed portions of Nescafé Original a day (2.3 ± 0.4 g per cup, ± unlabelled), made with boiled tap water to a 200 mL mark, intended to give 4 mg/kg body mass of caffeine a day; no measurement of the coffee's caffeine content is reported and the basis of the per-kg calculation is not stated (p. 3). Adherence: daily compliance booklets and serum caffeine on day 2, reported only as significantly higher in the coffee trial than the water trial (p<0.01), without values (p. 5).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: 4 × 200 mL black instant coffee (trial C) or 4 × 200 mL tap water (trial W) a day at fixed times (07:30–09:00, 10:30, 13:30, 16:30) for three trial days; test drinks totalled 800 mL a day in both trials. Caffeine during trial C: mean 308 mg a day, range 204.4–453.0 mg (p. 5). Daily fluid was set individually from the 3-day diary and provided as bottled water in six equal bottles at fixed times (whether the 800 mL of test drink counted within it is not stated, p. 3); mean water consumption during the trials 1953 ± 642 mL a day (± unlabelled, p. 5). Diet prescribed individually to match diary energy and fluid (50% carbohydrate, 35% fat, 15% protein) and replicated in the second trial (p. 3).
exposure.polysubstance: Alcohol prohibited from 24 h before and throughout each trial; smokers excluded; medicines containing caffeine excluded (pp. 2–3). The paper does not state whether the prescribed diet excluded other caffeine sources during the water trial, but day-2 serum caffeine was lower in the water trial (p. 5).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not an abstinence study. The water trial removed coffee for its three trial days in men who usually drank 3–6 cups a day (whether caffeine was also withheld on the control day is not stated); withdrawal symptoms were not measured. In the coffee trial the mean of 308 mg a day sat at the bottom of the 300–600 mg/day habitual range required for entry.

comparison.controls: Within-person: the same 50 men drinking the same volume (800 mL a day) of water instead of coffee, with identical diet and fluid prescription, in counterbalanced order.
comparison.matching: Self-matched (crossover); diet and fluid allocation replicated between trials (allocations amended during the first trial were repeated in the second, p. 7).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not a between-group comparison. Habitual caffeine intake was estimated only from the pre-study diary and questionnaire; individual tolerance to caffeine's effects on the kidney was not measured.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same people in both conditions; alcohol prohibited in both.

outcomes.instruments: Total body water by deuterium oxide dilution (0.1 g/kg D2O on the evenings of day 0 and day 2; serum enrichment by isotope-ratio mass spectrometry; divided by 1.04 to correct for non-exchangeable binding) on days 1 and 3; nude body mass each morning; urine: two 24-h collections (volume, specific gravity by refractometer, osmolality, creatinine, sodium, potassium) and three morning voids (volume, specific gravity); fasting blood on days 1–3 (haematocrit, serum osmolality, total plasma protein, serum sodium, potassium, creatinine, blood urea nitrogen); plasma caffeine on day 2 for adherence; Bristol Stool Chart and compliance booklet (pp. 3–4).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard laboratory hydration markers; the authors call deuterium-dilution total body water the gold standard (pp. 2, 4). No threshold (for example a urine specific gravity cut-off) was applied to classify anyone as dehydrated.
outcomes.operationalization: Dehydration was not defined in advance; it was operationalized as a statistically significant difference between conditions, or a change over time, in any marker. The discussion uses a 1–3% loss of body mass as the level of clinical dehydration (p. 6).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None reported across the 17 markers; two-way repeated-measures ANOVA with post hoc pairwise comparisons, and t-tests on day 1 to day 3 changes (p. 4).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Participants could not be blinded (coffee vs water); blinding of laboratory analysts not reported. Outcomes are objective laboratory or scale measurements, but the 24-h urine collections were made by participants who knew their condition.

analysis.effect_sizes: Means with ± values (SDs in the tables, unlabelled in the text) and p-values only; no between-condition differences with confidence intervals. 24-h urine volume, mean of the two collections (editors' arithmetic): coffee 2409 ± 660 vs water 2428 ± 669 mL (abstract, p. 1; ± unlabelled, read as SD); by collection (Table 3, p. 6): first 2593 (SD 833) vs 2521 (SD 744), second 2226 (SD 842) vs 2335 (SD 826) mL. Editors' calculation from the abstract values: difference −19 mL a day (coffee minus water); treating the two trials as independent groups, which can only widen the interval when a man's two trials are positively correlated, the 95% interval is about −290 to +250 mL a day (−286 to +248 with t on 49 df). Total body water 51.5 ± 1.4 vs 51.4 ± 1.3 kg, dispersion measure not stated, probably standard errors of the 25 men of Figure 2 (p. 1); condition p=0.90, trial day p=0.43 (p. 5). Body mass: no condition difference (p=0.45); fall from day 1 to day 3 of 0.39 ± 0.5 kg across both trials, p<0.05 (p. 5). Urinary sodium 48.7 vs 43.6 mmol/24 h (first collection) and 47.0 vs 43.4 (second), p=0.02 (pp. 5–6); editors' calculation: 3.6–5.1 mmol a day (8–12%) more with coffee. Morning void volume p=0.86, specific gravity p=0.95 (p. 5).
analysis.covariates: None. Two-way repeated-measures ANOVA (condition × day) and paired t-tests on changes; period (order) effects not reported.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No trial registration or protocol is mentioned in the paper.
analysis.selective_reporting: All 17 markers are tabulated or plotted, but total body water, the measure the authors call the gold standard, appears only as a bar chart for 25 of the 50 participants with no explanation, and the abstract's total-body-water values do not say whether ± is an SD or a standard error. Serum caffeine values are not given. Period effects and within-person differences are not reported.
analysis.power: No sample-size or power calculation. Within-person differences and their variability are not reported, so the smallest detectable difference cannot be computed from the paper; the editors' conservative bound above indicates that the 24-h urine data make a coffee-induced excess of more than about 250 mL a day unlikely but cannot exclude a smaller one.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 50 healthy men who habitually drank 3–6 cups of coffee a day, three days of 800 mL a day of instant coffee (mean 308 mg caffeine) produced no statistically significant difference from the same volume of water in 24-h urine volume, urine concentration, morning urine, blood markers, body mass or total body water (the last shown for 25 men). Urinary sodium was 8–12% higher with coffee without more urine. Body mass fell slightly, by 0.39 kg over two days, in both conditions alike.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title says there is no evidence of dehydration, and the abstract concludes that coffee drunk in moderation by caffeine-habituated men "provides similar hydrating qualities to water" (p. 1); the discussion says public-health advice on coffee and hydration should be updated (p. 7). Gaps: (1) 'similar' is a claim of equivalence, but no equivalence margin, confidence interval or power calculation is given, only non-significant p-values; (2) the gold-standard total-body-water result rests on 25 of 50 men, which the abstract does not say; (3) the population was men already habituated to caffeine, given an amount at the bottom of their usual intake, so the result does not reach people who rarely consume caffeine, women, or larger intakes, which the authors' own summary of earlier studies links to diuresis (pp. 1–2); (4) a change in public-health advice is asked for on the basis of one three-day study in 50 men. The headline 'coffee hydrates as well as water' is fair for habitual moderate coffee drinkers drinking their usual amount and overstated as a general rule. The study was funded by the Institute for Scientific Information on Coffee and one author was employed by PepsiCo (p. 1), recorded as a flag.

timeline.event: Eddy & Downs: early report of tolerance to the diuretic effect of caffeine with regular consumption (cited in the introduction, p. 1).

Neuhauser-Berthold et al.: six cups of coffee after five days without caffeine were followed by a 2.7% fall in total body water and 41% more urine over 24 h (as described by Killer et al., p. 2; caffeine given as 624 mg in the text and 642 mg in Table 1).

Grandjean et al.: no effect of caffeinated drinks including coffee, compared with non-caffeinated drinks, on hydration markers in 18 caffeine-habituated adults; total body water not measured (as described, pp. 2, 6).
Armstrong et al.: 226 and 452 mg caffeine in people habitually consuming about 98 mg/day, no diuretic effect (Table 1, p. 2).
Silva et al.: caffeine 5 mg/kg a day or placebo for four days in 30 men consuming under 100 mg/day, no change in total body water (as described, pp. 2, 6).
This trial: no detectable difference between 800 mL a day of instant coffee and of water over three days in 50 caffeine-habituated men.

replication.where_it_stands: The finding agrees with the earlier controlled studies its authors cite in caffeine-habituated people at moderate amounts, while studies after several days without caffeine or at larger amounts reported diuresis (Table 1, p. 2; second-hand, not appraised). These are conceptual, not direct, replications, and no later study was read for this card. What remains open is the size of any small effect and whether the result holds for women, people who rarely consume caffeine and larger intakes.

funding.funder: Institute for Scientific Information on Coffee (ISIC), described in the paper as a non-profit organisation devoted to the study and disclosure of science on coffee and health; the paper states the funder had no role in design, data collection and analysis, the decision to publish or the manuscript (p. 1).
funding.declared_conflicts: Killer and Blannin declared no competing interests. Jeukendrup was employed by PepsiCo Inc. at the time and was an adjunct professor at the University of Birmingham; the paper states the views are the authors' and not PepsiCo's (p. 1).
funding.affiliations_note: The paper does not say who funds ISIC. The funder's coffee focus and an author's employment by a beverage company are recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered randomized crossover equivalence trial with a prespecified margin for 24-h urine output and body water, in women and men who do and do not habitually consume caffeine, comparing coffee, decaffeinated coffee and water at more than one amount, with complete total-body-water data and within-person differences reported with confidence intervals.

domains.domain: Randomization process
domains.note: Participants were randomly allocated to a counterbalanced order (p. 3), but sequence generation and allocation concealment are not described; day-1 values are similar in the two conditions (Tables 3–5, Figure 2).

domains.domain: Bias arising from period and carryover effects (crossover)
domains.note: A 10-day washout on usual diet and caffeine makes carryover of hydration effects unlikely, but the number of participants in each sequence and any period effect are not reported, and the analysis did not include period.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Open-label by necessity in a free-living setting. Adherence rests on self-report booklets and a day-2 serum caffeine difference reported without values; participants could return during the first trial to have their water allocation changed, the adjusted amount then being repeated in the second trial (p. 7), and how many did so is not reported.

domains.domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
domains.note: 2 of 52 dropped out and per-marker data are missing for up to 8 of 50 (urine potassium, 42); total body water is shown for only 25 participants with no reason given. Nothing suggests missingness depended on the true values, but there is no sensitivity analysis.

domains.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Objective laboratory and scale measurements, identical in both conditions; the 24-h urine collections depended on participants who knew their condition, a minor concern.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No registration or prespecified primary outcome; all markers are reported, but total body water appears only as a 25-person bar chart with unlabelled error bars, and no within-person differences or intervals are given.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A well-controlled crossover with objective markers, but reporting gaps (randomization details, period effects, total body water in half the sample, no intervals) leave some concerns in several domains. The design supports the statement that, in caffeine-habituated healthy men, 800 mL a day of instant coffee did not detectably change three-day hydration markers relative to water; it cannot support equivalence or extension to women, people who rarely consume caffeine or larger intakes. Cite it for the absence of a detectable difference in this population, not for coffee hydrating exactly like water.

key_findings.finding: Who and what: 52 healthy non-smoking men aged 18–46 who habitually drank 3–6 cups of coffee a day (300–600 mg/day caffeine by 3-day weighed diary) were enrolled; 50 completed both arms: three days of four 200 mL mugs of black instant coffee a day (4 mg/kg/day caffeine by design) and three days of four 200 mL mugs of water, with an individually prescribed diet replicated in both trials and each man's daily fluid, set from his diary, provided as bottled water in six equal bottles (whether the 800 mL of test drink counted within it is not stated), separated by a 10-day washout.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 1); Methods › Participants (p. 2, continuing on p. 3); Study Design; Treatment, 1st paragraph; Beverages (p. 3); Results › Participant Characteristics (p. 4)
key_findings.note: Enrolment (52) and completion (50) are spelled out in words on pp. 2 and 4; 50 is in digits in the abstract. Only urine volume and specific gravity (24-h collections and morning voids) and body mass (Figure 3) are reported for all 50; the other urine and blood markers for 42–49 each, total body water for 25 (Figure 2), and blood urea nitrogen and serum caffeine without a number (pp. 4–6).

key_findings.finding: Caffeine in the coffee trial as reported: mean 308 mg a day (range 204.4–453.0 mg), at the bottom of the 300–600 mg/day habitual range required for entry. No measurement of the coffee's caffeine content is reported, and the mean and minimum equal 4 mg/kg of the mean (77.0 kg) and minimum (51.1 kg) weights in Table 2 (editors' arithmetic), so they look calculated rather than measured. Test drinks totalled 800 mL a day in both trials, and water during the trials averaged 1953 ± 642 mL a day (± unlabelled).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Beverages (p. 3); Results › Dietary Intakes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (the 2nd continuing on p. 5) and 5th paragraph (p. 5); Table 2 (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Daily urine output did not differ: 2409 ± 660 mL with coffee vs 2428 ± 669 mL with water (abstract; ± unlabelled, consistent with SDs given the per-collection SDs of 744–842 mL in Table 3; the means equal the averages of the two 24-h collections, editors' arithmetic); by collection 2593 vs 2521 mL and 2226 vs 2335 mL. 24-h urine specific gravity was 1.009 in every condition and collection, and osmolality and creatinine did not differ either (p>0.05).
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 1); Results › Urinary Markers, 1st paragraph (p. 5); Table 3 (p. 6)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: difference −19 mL a day; treating the two trials as independent groups, which can only widen the interval when a man's two trials are positively correlated, the 95% interval is about −290 to +250 mL a day (−286 to +248 with t on 49 df), so a coffee-induced excess above about 250 mL a day is unlikely but a smaller one is not excluded. The paper reports no interval. Volume and specific gravity are reported for all 50 men, osmolality for 46 and creatinine for 48 (p. 4).

key_findings.finding: The one difference: urinary sodium excretion was higher with coffee in both collections, 48.7 vs 43.6 mmol/24 h and 47.0 vs 43.4 mmol/24 h (p=0.02), without more urine; the authors attribute it to the sodium-excreting action of caffeine and related methylxanthines on the kidney described in earlier studies.
key_findings.locator: Results › Urinary Markers, 1st paragraph (p. 5, right column); Table 3; Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 6)
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: 3.6–5.1 mmol a day, 8–12% more with coffee.

key_findings.finding: Total body water by deuterium dilution showed no significant change from day 1 to day 3 in either trial (p>0.05) and no difference between trials (condition p=0.90; trial day p=0.43); the abstract gives 51.5 ± 1.4 vs 51.4 ± 1.3 kg for coffee vs water (± unlabelled), but Figure 2 shows these data for n=25, not the 50 completers.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 1); Results › Body Mass Variables, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 (p. 5)
key_findings.note: Read from Figure 2 at 300 dpi (approximate): coffee about 50.7 kg before and 52.2 kg after, water about 51.0 and 51.65 kg; error bars about ±1.3–1.5 kg, unlabelled. The averages of the two time points (editors' reading: 51.44 ± 1.46 and 51.35 ± 1.33 kg) match the abstract's values within reading precision, so those probably also rest on the 25 men, and their ± fit standard errors (implied SD about 7 kg). Total body water thus rose numerically in both trials while body mass fell, which suggests measurement noise of the order of a kilogram.

key_findings.finding: Nude morning body mass (76.97 ± 12.15 kg, n=50) did not differ between conditions (p=0.45) but fell slightly in both, by 0.39 ± 0.5 kg from day 1 to day 3 across trials (p<0.05); the discussion expresses this as 190 ± 120 g a day, 0.2% of body mass, against the 1–3% loss it cites as clinical dehydration. These ± values are unlabelled and are read as SDs (see reporting issues).
key_findings.locator: Results › Body Mass Variables, 2nd paragraph (p. 5); Figure 3; Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 6)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: the cumulative fall of 0.39 kg is about 0.5% of 76.97 kg, still well below 1%.

key_findings.finding: Fasting blood markers did not differ between conditions, and their changes from day 1 to day 3 did not differ between conditions either: haematocrit 43.9–44.6%, serum osmolality 284–288 mOsm/kg and serum sodium 141 mmol/L on every day of both trials; total plasma protein and serum potassium likewise, and serum creatinine did not differ between conditions or days.

key_findings.finding: Morning urine volume (338.3–361.9 mL) and specific gravity (1.017–1.019) did not differ between conditions (p=0.86 and p=0.95).

key_findings.finding: Adherence rested on daily booklets (all participants reported eating and drinking what was provided, no exercise beyond walking, no diarrhoea or vomiting) and on day-2 serum caffeine, reported only as higher in the coffee trial (p<0.01) without values.

key_findings.finding: The authors list as limitations the free-living setting rather than a metabolic ward, no 24-h urine collection on the third day, and no decaffeinated-coffee arm, which they judge unlikely to have changed the result.

key_findings.finding: The authors' own summary of 13 earlier results (Table 1) lists a diuretic effect in 7 and none in 6; the introduction reads them as showing diuresis with large amounts (stated as 500 mg or more) and in people without recent caffeine, and none at low to moderate amounts.

reporting_issues.issue: The text states that haematological markers did not differ between conditions and gives '(p<0.05)'; for a null result this should read p>0.05.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 5 labels serum creatinine in mmol/L, with values of 95.2–98.9; values of this size fit µmol/L.
reporting_issues.consequence: Unit error; no effect on the comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: Total body water, described as the gold-standard measure, is shown for n=25 (Figure 2) although 50 completed; the list of per-marker sample sizes omits it and no reason is given. The abstract does not say so, and its values match the averages of the pre- and post-trial bars of Figure 2 (editors' reading at 300 dpi: 51.44 ± 1.46 and 51.35 ± 1.33 kg), so they probably rest on the same 25 men.
reporting_issues.consequence: The total-body-water result rests on half the sample, selected in an unreported way, and is less precise than the abstract implies.

reporting_issues.issue: No ± value in the abstract or the running text is labelled; only Tables 2–5 say SD. Total body water is given as 51.5±1.4 vs 51.4±1.3 kg in the abstract: with a body-weight SD of 12.1 kg (Table 2), an SD of 1.4 kg for total body water would be implausibly small, and the error bars of Figures 2 and 3 are standard errors on the editors' reading (Figure 3: about ±1.7 kg for body mass, n=50, against a printed SD of 12.15 kg, whose standard error is 1.72). The other text values fit SDs on the editors' arithmetic: urine volume 2409±660 and 2428±669 mL, body mass 76.97±12.15 kg, its fall 0.39±0.5 kg (0.4±0.5 kg in the abstract) and 190±120 g a day, water 1953±642 mL, energy 2425±413 kcal and coffee 2.3±0.4 g per cup; read as standard errors they would imply spreads of several litres or kilograms, or a body-mass fall that was not significant.
reporting_issues.consequence: Read as SDs, the total-body-water values would overstate how tightly it was measured; read as standard errors they imply an SD of about 7 kg (editors' calculation, 1.4 × √25). The card writes the other text values with ± and reads them as SDs.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion states that baseline urinary potassium was significantly higher on day one of the coffee trial than of the water trial, but the Results report no between-condition difference in potassium and Table 3 marks only a day effect (32.3 vs 36.6 mmol/24 h in the first collection, no asterisk).
reporting_issues.consequence: Text contradicts the Results and the table; the discussion's potassium explanation (about 320 mg extra potassium from four cups) rests on a difference the Results do not report.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says each trial lasted three consecutive days; the Methods say each treatment lasted four consecutive days (a control day plus three trial days, Figure 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; coffee or water was given on three trial days.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods place the 24-h urine collections on trial days 2–3; the Results and Table 3 label them days 1 and 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Labelling inconsistency (start or end day of each collection); no effect on the comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: The body-mass fall is given as 0.39±0.5 kg from day 1 to day 3 (Results; 0.4±0.5 kg in the abstract) and as 190±120 g a day (Discussion). Read as SDs, 120 g a day implies a two-day SD of at most about 240 g, not 500 g (editors' arithmetic). The abstract places the 0.4 kg after 'a small progressive daily fall', so it can be read as a daily loss about twice the reported one, although it is the two-day total. The discussion compares the daily 0.2% with the 1–3% threshold of clinical dehydration; the cumulative fall is about 0.5% of body mass.
reporting_issues.consequence: The spread of the body-mass fall is uncertain; the conclusion that it is far below clinical dehydration holds either way.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say total body water was analysed by gas chromatography mass spectrometry, the Methods describe isotope-ratio mass spectrometry, and the introduction calls doubly labelled water dilution the gold standard although the study used deuterium oxide alone.
reporting_issues.consequence: Descriptive inconsistencies in the method; no effect on the results.
