design_detail: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group laboratory study on a single test day (University of Bristol, UK). 369 adults aged 18–62, grouped by questionnaire-estimated habitual caffeine intake into 'non-low' (under 40 mg/day, n=157) and 'medium-high' (40 mg/day or more, n=212) consumers, abstained from caffeine from 7 PM the evening before (checked by salivary caffeine); after a baseline test battery at 10:30 AM they were randomly assigned to caffeine capsules (100 mg at 11:15 AM, 150 mg at 12:45 PM) or placebo. The battery (tapping speed; self-rated mental alertness, sleepiness and anxiety/jitteriness; recognition memory; simple and choice reaction time) was repeated three times, and the results reported in detail are the means of the two runs after the second dose (1:45–3:30 PM). Treatment was randomized; consumer status was not, so the 2 × 2 design mixes a randomized comparison (caffeine vs placebo) with an observational one (consumer groups). Part of a larger protocol from which some data were reported earlier (Rogers et al., 2010).
can_establish: The acute effect of 250 mg of caffeine (100 + 150 mg) versus placebo, within each consumer group after overnight abstinence, on these self-ratings and simple tasks, which is a randomized comparison.
cannot_establish: That the poorer state of medium-high consumers on placebo was caused by caffeine withdrawal, or that tolerance explains the group differences (consumer groups were self-selected and differ in ways not all measured); effects of other amounts, times of day or everyday patterns of consumption; or effects on complex thinking (mental performance was measured as errors on two simple tasks and as reaction times).

sample.recruitment: Volunteers in a larger protocol at the University of Bristol (described in Rogers et al., 2010, not read); this report includes only the 369 whose salivary caffeine confirmed their consumer status and overnight abstinence and who had complete data (p. 231). How participants were recruited is not described in this paper.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18–62; non-smokers or light smokers (≤5 cigarettes or equivalent a day; no smoking on the test day until leaving the laboratory) (p. 231). Excluded on baseline salivary caffeine: non-low consumers above 0.2 µg/ml and medium-high consumers above 2.0 µg/ml (p. 233). Other criteria are given in Rogers et al. (2010).
sample.demographics: Non-low vs medium-high consumers: caffeine intake 10.2 (SD 11.6) vs 235 (SD 146) mg/day; age 31.7 (SD 12.1) vs 33.8 (SD 12.7) years; 85 of 157 vs 109 of 212 women; 21 vs 41 smokers. Baseline salivary caffeine 0.019 (SD 0.036, maximum 0.17) vs 0.29 (SD 0.38, maximum 1.97) µg/ml; paraxanthine 0.021 (SD 0.036) vs 0.29 (SD 0.30) µg/ml (p. 233). Education and ethnicity not reported.
sample.attrition: Not reported in this paper: the numbers tested, randomized and excluded for salivary caffeine or incomplete data are not given (p. 231). 42% of the non-low group had detectable caffeine and/or paraxanthine in saliva (p. 235).
sample.selection_effects: Consumer groups are self-selected; the analysis set is restricted to people with complete data and salivary values inside the cut-offs. The 'non-low' group is not caffeine-free (mean 10.2 mg/day; 42% with detectable caffeine or paraxanthine), and the 'medium-high' group begins at 40 mg/day, so it spans light to heavy consumption.

exposure.measurement: Habitual intake: questionnaire on how often caffeine-containing products were consumed in the week before testing, converted to mg/day from published caffeine contents; the 40 mg/day cut-off was supported by the authors' earlier analyses of four consumption levels in the same cohort (p. 231). Overnight abstinence checked by salivary caffeine at 11:10 AM (p. 233). Treatment: caffeine BP anhydrous powder or cornflour placebo in identical white size-1 capsules, double-blind (p. 231).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: 100 mg caffeine at 11:15 AM and 150 mg at 12:45 PM by mouth (250 mg in total), or placebo at both times, after abstinence from at least 7 PM the previous evening; the authors chose the two doses to model afternoon caffeine levels after two to three cups of ground coffee earlier in the day (p. 231). Test battery at 10:30 AM (baseline), 45 min after the first dose, and 60 and 135 min after the second dose (p. 232).
exposure.polysubstance: Light smoking (≤5 a day) allowed outside the test day; smoking status was a covariate (21 non-low vs 41 medium-high smokers). Alcohol and other drug use not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: From at least 7 PM the previous evening, checked by salivary caffeine. Editors' calculation: about 15.5 h at the 10:30 AM baseline and about 19–20.5 h at the afternoon tests for those on placebo. The authors note that in everyday life regular consumers typically take caffeine from soon after waking (p. 239), so the afternoon placebo condition is a longer abstinence than usual.

comparison.controls: For the caffeine effect: placebo within the same consumer group (randomized). For the 'withdrawal' effect: non-low consumers given placebo, used by the authors as the benchmark of normal functioning for the time of day (not randomized) (p. 231).
comparison.matching: None between consumer groups; gender as a fixed factor and age and smoking status as covariates in all analyses; baseline scores as covariates in analyses run separately within each consumer group (p. 232).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measure of how alert, sleepy, anxious or fast people were before they began consuming caffeine; prior-night sleep, chronotype, personality, education and other drug use not reported. The authors address self-selection by citing earlier studies in which caffeine consumers were randomized to acute or long-term withdrawal (p. 238), not with data from this study.

outcomes.instruments: Computer battery (E-Prime, about 30 min, run four times): tapping speed (space-bar taps in 30 s); self-ratings on 1–9 scales rescaled to 0–8 of mental alertness (mentally alert/attentive/able to concentrate/observant), sleepiness (sleepy/drowsy/half awake) and anxiety/jitteriness (anxious/tense/nervous/on edge with jittery/shaky); recognition memory (total errors over six series of five digits with 30 probes each); simple reaction time (64 trials, variable foreperiod, analysed in four blocks); two-choice reaction time (384 trials; mean reaction time and errors) (pp. 231–232).
outcomes.validity_norms: Rating items come from the authors' Mood, Alertness and Physical Sensations Scales, modelled on Goldstein et al. (1969); no psychometric validation is reported here. No population norms: 'normal' is defined as the non-low placebo group.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Withdrawal effect' = poorer scores of medium-high consumers on placebo than of non-low consumers on placebo. 'Net benefit' = caffeine bringing scores beyond the non-low placebo level. 'Smarter' = fewer errors on the recognition-memory and choice-reaction tasks; 'faster' = tapping speed and reaction times.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Tukey HSD for pairwise group comparisons within each measure; no correction across the 8 measures, the test runs or the additional regression analyses.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Treatment double-blind; tasks and ratings computer-administered. Participants knew they had abstained overnight, which the authors note could lower medium-high consumers' self-rated alertness (p. 235).

analysis.effect_sizes: ANOVA F tests, df 1,363 at baseline and 1,359 after treatment (Table 1, p. 234); group means with SEs shown only as bars in Figure 1 (p. 233). Caffeine main effects: sleepiness F=26.50 and anxiety/jitteriness F=16.78 (both p<0.0001), mental alertness F=10.75 (p=0.001), simple reaction time F=26.84 (p<0.0001), choice reaction time F=10.92 (p=0.001), choice errors F=8.87 (p=0.003), recognition memory F=3.41 (p=0.065), tapping F=9.89 (p=0.002). Caffeine × consumer status: anxiety/jitteriness F=18.66 (p<0.0001), mental alertness F=13.05 (p=0.0003), simple reaction time F=10.89 (p=0.001), recognition memory F=6.23 (p=0.013), choice reaction time F=3.30 (p=0.07), choice errors F=2.92 (p=0.09), sleepiness F=1.79 (p>0.1), tapping F<1. The authors estimate that withdrawal slowed simple reaction time by 52 ms against a non-low placebo SD of 58 ms and call this large (p. 237); editors' calculation: about 0.9 SD, and the printed arithmetic (485−417)−(437−420) gives 51 ms. Standardized regression coefficients for change scores in those given caffeine: Table 2 (p. 235). No confidence intervals are reported.
analysis.covariates: Gender (fixed factor), age and smoking status in all analyses; baseline score as covariate in the analyses run within each consumer group (p. 232).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol mentioned. The data come from a larger protocol, some of which was reported in Rogers et al. (2010), where sleepiness and alertness were not treated separately (p. 231).
analysis.selective_reporting: Only the post-second-dose results (mean of runs 3 and 4) are reported in detail, to simplify the presentation (p. 232); the run 45 min after the first dose (100 mg) is described only as giving broadly similar but smaller effects, data not shown (p. 236). The 40 mg/day grouping was supported by earlier analyses of the same cohort (p. 231), so the cut-off was chosen with knowledge of the data. Several further analyses are reported as data not shown (pp. 234, 238).
analysis.power: Not reported; 77 to 106 participants per cell. The authors attribute other studies' failure to find consumer-group differences partly to low statistical power (p. 235).

interpretation_gap.results_show: On placebo in the afternoon, after about 19–20 hours without caffeine, medium-high consumers were sleepier, less mentally alert, slower on simple reaction time (485 vs 437 ms) and made more errors than non-low consumers on placebo; caffeine brought them back to about the non-low placebo level but not beyond it. In non-low consumers caffeine reduced sleepiness and raised anxiety/jitteriness (from about 0.7 to 1.6 on the 0–8 scale, read from Figure 1) without changing mental alertness or errors. Caffeine increased tapping speed by about 6–7 taps per 30 s in both groups. At the 10:30 AM baseline the group differences were small (simple reaction time 391 vs 402 ms).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that tolerance to caffeine's effects on sleepiness "means that frequent consumption fails to enhance mental alertness and mental performance" (p. 229), and the discussion that the group differences reflect recent caffeine exposure rather than individual differences that predate it (p. 238). Gaps: (1) the withdrawal and tolerance interpretation rests on comparing self-selected groups; the abstract does not say so, the discussion states that the results strongly support the no-net-benefit account and demonstrate adverse effects of overnight withdrawal that worsen into the afternoon (p. 235), the final comments present complete tolerance to the effects on sleepiness and anxiety/jitteriness as established (p. 238), and the discussion supports this with other studies that randomized consumers to acute or long-term withdrawal (p. 238), not with these data; (2) the decisive afternoon tests came after 19–20 hours without caffeine, longer than in everyday life (p. 239); (3) one dose regimen (250 mg) at one time of day was tested; the authors themselves mention that lower doses might favour alertness in people who rarely consume caffeine (p. 236); (4) 'smarter' means two simple error counts; (5) the abstract calls the anxiety increase in non-low consumers substantial, but it is about one point on a 0–8 scale from a low level. A headline 'coffee only fixes the withdrawal it causes' goes beyond this single-session study with non-randomized groups. What the data support is narrower: caffeine made regular consumers faster but, on these simple tasks, no more accurate than people who rarely consume caffeine given placebo.

timeline.event: Hollingworth: 15 people over 45 days; caffeine increased tapping speed and, at the highest dose, impaired coordination; the authors argue the design may have confounded caffeine with withdrawal (pp. 229–230).

Goldstein et al.: 18 women who did not drink coffee vs 38 who drank at least five cups a day; the coffee drinkers felt less alert before treatment and caffeine raised their alertness only to the non-drinkers' placebo level; little effect in non-drinkers (as described, p. 230).

Richardson et al.: caffeine consumers randomized to acute or long-term withdrawal; morning sleepiness was the same in non-low consumers and long-term-withdrawn consumers and rose only after acute withdrawal (as described, p. 238).

James & Rogers: withdrawal-reversal account of caffeine's effects on performance and mood, the basis of this study's hypotheses (p. 231); disputed by Dews et al. (2002), Haskell et al. (2005), Smith et al. (2006) and Childs & de Wit (2006) (p. 230).

Haskell et al. (2005) and Smith et al. (2006): no consumer-group differences in morning alertness or performance; their 'non-consumers' had higher baseline salivary caffeine than this study's non-low group (as described, p. 235).
Sigmon et al.: long-term versus acute withdrawal; afternoon tiredness rose only after acute withdrawal and caffeine reduced it equally in both (as described, p. 238).
Rogers et al.: earlier report from the same cohort and protocol (genetic variants and habitual intake); not independent of this paper (pp. 231–232).
This study: caffeine restored medium-high consumers on placebo to the non-low placebo level and sped tapping in both groups.

replication.where_it_stands: Contested. This large (n=369) laboratory comparison supports withdrawal reversal for mental alertness and simple task accuracy, while studies by other groups found no consumer-group differences (Haskell et al., 2005; Smith et al., 2006, as described here). It shares its cohort with Rogers et al. (2010) and must not be counted as independent of it. The project's caffeine reading list holds the published exchange on withdrawal reversal (for example Smith's 2008 reply to James, James 2014 and Rogers 2014), not read for this card.

funding.affiliations_note: The study tests the withdrawal-reversal account set out by the first author with James (James and Rogers, 2005), which the paper names as the basis of its hypotheses (p. 231); recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered trial that randomizes regular caffeine consumers to keep consuming caffeine or to stop for several weeks (checked by salivary caffeine), then tests caffeine and placebo at several doses and times of day in both arms and in people who rarely consume caffeine, with demanding cognitive tasks as well as reaction time, so that tolerance and withdrawal are tested within randomized groups instead of being inferred from self-selected ones.

domains.domain: Randomization process
domains.note: Random assignment to caffeine or placebo within consumer groups is stated (p. 231), but sequence generation, allocation concealment, placebo-group sizes and baseline values by treatment arm are not reported here; baseline differences were handled by covariance.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Identical capsules, double-blind, given in the laboratory.

domains.domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
domains.note: Analysis restricted to participants with complete data and salivary values inside the cut-offs; how many were randomized and excluded is not reported here.

domains.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Computer-administered tasks and self-ratings by participants blind to treatment. Knowing they had abstained (the authors' caveat, p. 235) may affect the consumer-group comparison, not the caffeine–placebo contrast.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No registration; only the post-second-dose runs are reported in detail; first-dose results and several analyses are data not shown; the 40 mg/day grouping was chosen after earlier analyses of the same cohort.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: RoB 2 applies to the randomized caffeine-versus-placebo contrast, which is well blinded; some concerns arise from unreported randomization details, unreported exclusions and selective presentation of time points. The comparisons between consumer groups, which carry the withdrawal and tolerance interpretation and the 'no net benefit' conclusion, are not randomized: by ROBINS-E standards they would be at high risk of bias from confounding (self-selection, adjusted only for gender, age and smoking). Cite the study for the acute effects of 250 mg of caffeine within each group and for the pattern observed across groups; cite withdrawal reversal as the authors' interpretation.

key_findings.finding: Who: 369 adults aged 18–62, 157 'non-low' consumers (questionnaire intake under 40 mg/day, mean 10.2) and 212 'medium-high' consumers (40 mg/day or more, mean 235), randomly assigned to caffeine (77 and 106) or placebo; all had abstained from caffeine from 7 PM the previous evening, checked by salivary caffeine.
key_findings.locator: Method › Participants; Design and treatments (p. 231); Procedure (p. 232); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 233); Table 2 (p. 235)
key_findings.note: Placebo-group sizes (80 and 106) are not printed; editors' subtraction from the totals.

key_findings.finding: Conditions: caffeine 100 mg at 11:15 AM and 150 mg at 12:45 PM in identical capsules, or cornflour placebo, double-blind; the results reported in detail are the means of two test runs 60 and 135 min after the second dose, between 1:45 and 3:30 PM.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 229); Method › Design and treatments (p. 231); Procedure; Data analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 232)

key_findings.finding: At the 10:30 AM baseline, after overnight abstinence, medium-high consumers were slightly slower on simple reaction time (402 vs 391 ms, p=0.03) and made more choice-reaction errors (9.92 vs 8.18, p=0.02); differences in sleepiness (2.35 vs 2.01, p=0.09), mental alertness (5.02 vs 5.33, p=0.08), choice reaction time, recognition memory and tapping were not significant, and the authors call the baseline differences small.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, pre-treatment baseline column (p. 234); Discussion › Effects of acute caffeine abstinence, 1st paragraph (p. 235)

key_findings.finding: In the afternoon, medium-high consumers given placebo were the odd group out: sleepiest, least mentally alert, slowest on simple reaction time (485 ms vs 437 ms in non-low consumers on placebo) and most error-prone. Given caffeine, they did not differ significantly from non-low consumers on placebo on any measure where Figure 1 shows letters (sleepiness, mental alertness, simple reaction time and both error counts) and were no better than them on alertness or errors, while their reaction times were numerically faster (simple 417 vs 437 ms; choice about 462 vs 479 ms), which the authors attribute to caffeine's motor effect.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 233, right column); Figure 1a–g (p. 233); Discussion › Faster but not smarter, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (p. 237)
key_findings.note: Simple reaction times are printed in the text (p. 237). Other values read from Figure 1 at 300 dpi (approximate): sleepiness about 3.7 (medium-high placebo) vs 2.8 (non-low placebo) and 2.5 (medium-high caffeine); mental alertness about 3.5 vs 4.6 and 4.65; choice-reaction errors about 15.5 vs 11.3 and 11.4; recognition-memory errors about 13.5 vs 8.4 and 8.8. Choice reaction time read from Figure 1e (approximate): about 479 (non-low placebo, a bar without a letter), 467 (non-low caffeine), 494 (medium-high placebo) and 462 ms (medium-high caffeine).

key_findings.finding: In non-low consumers, caffeine reduced sleepiness and increased anxiety/jitteriness but did not change mental alertness or the number of errors on the recognition-memory and choice-reaction tasks; it sped up tapping and, to a smaller extent, simple reaction time (420 vs 437 ms) and choice reaction time.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 233, continuing on p. 234); Figure 1 (p. 233); Discussion › Faster but not smarter, 4th paragraph (p. 237)
key_findings.note: From Figure 1b (approximate): anxiety/jitteriness about 0.7 on placebo vs 1.6 on caffeine in non-low consumers, about 1.1 vs 1.05 in medium-high consumers, on the 0–8 scale.

key_findings.finding: Caffeine × consumer-status interactions were significant for anxiety/jitteriness (F=18.66, p<0.0001), mental alertness (F=13.05, p=0.0003), simple reaction time (F=10.89, p=0.001) and recognition memory (F=6.23, p=0.013), but not for sleepiness (F=1.79, p>0.1) or tapping (F<1); the overall caffeine effect on recognition memory was not significant (p=0.065).
key_findings.locator: Table 1

key_findings.finding: 'Faster': caffeine increased tapping speed by 6.1 (non-low) and 6.7 (medium-high) taps per 30 s, and tapping did not differ between the consumer groups on placebo, so the authors read caffeine's motor effect as independent of habitual intake.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1h (p. 233); Table 1 (p. 234); Discussion › Faster but not smarter, 2nd and 4th paragraphs (p. 237)
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of Figure 1h: placebo tapping about 178–181 taps per 30 s, so the gain is roughly 3–4%.

key_findings.finding: The authors estimate that withdrawal slowed simple reaction time by 52 ms in medium-high consumers, assuming caffeine's purely motor speeding (17 ms in non-low consumers) is the same in both groups; against the non-low placebo SD of 58 ms they call this a large effect.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Faster but not smarter, 4th paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: about 0.9 SD. The printed arithmetic (485−417)−(437−420) gives 51 ms, not 52 (see reporting issues). The estimate combines a randomized contrast with a non-randomized one.

key_findings.finding: On the simple reaction-time task, medium-high consumers given placebo slowed progressively over the four blocks (caffeine × consumer status × block F(2.44, 874.8)=3.51, p=0.02), while the other three groups did not; the authors read this as a vigilance decrement caused by withdrawal.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Figure 2

key_findings.finding: Among those given caffeine, the change in mental alertness was predicted by the change in sleepiness in both groups (standardized β −0.35 non-low, n=77; −0.47 medium-high, n=106) and by the change in anxiety/jitteriness only in non-low consumers (β −0.38 vs −0.07); the effects of caffeine on sleepiness and on anxiety/jitteriness were unrelated (r=0.07 and r=0.04).
key_findings.locator: Results, 5th paragraph (p. 234, from the foot of the left column into the right column); Table 2 (p. 235)

key_findings.finding: Salivary checks: baseline caffeine was 0.019 (SD 0.036) µg/ml in non-low and 0.29 (SD 0.38) µg/ml in medium-high consumers, but 42% of the non-low group still had detectable caffeine and/or paraxanthine; the authors argue that misclassification of this kind would make group differences smaller, not larger.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 233); Discussion › Effects of acute caffeine abstinence, 1st paragraph (p. 235, right column)

key_findings.finding: The authors acknowledge two possible biases bearing on the consumer-group differences: the groups are self-selected, so individual differences could explain the findings, and knowing they had abstained could lower medium-high consumers' self-rated alertness and raise their sleepiness (performance, they argue, less so). Against pre-existing differences they cite other studies, not data from this study: Richardson et al. (1995), in which consumers were randomized to acute or long-term withdrawal, and Sigmon et al. (2009), comparing long-term with acute withdrawal (randomization not stated in this paper); they judge it reasonable to conclude that the effects reflect recent caffeine exposure.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Effects of acute caffeine abstinence, 2nd paragraph (p. 235); Non-low caffeine consumers as a model for studying the effects of caffeine—possible sources of bias, 1st and 4th paragraphs (p. 238)

key_findings.finding: Only the results after the second dose are reported in detail; after 100 mg alone, effects in non-low consumers were described as broadly similar but somewhat smaller, with a small non-significant rise in mental alertness (data not shown).
key_findings.locator: Method › Data analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 232); Discussion › Explaining the effects of caffeine and caffeine withdrawal on mental alertness, 3rd paragraph (p. 236, right column)

reporting_issues.issue: The withdrawal slowing of simple reaction time is given as 52 ms; editors' arithmetic on the printed calculation, (485−417)−(437−420), gives 51 ms.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably rounding of the group means; the size of the estimate (about 0.9 SD) is unchanged.

reporting_issues.issue: The sizes of the placebo groups and the baseline characteristics of the caffeine and placebo arms are not reported; only the caffeine-group sizes (77 and 106) appear, in Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Balance between randomized arms cannot be checked; placebo-group sizes can only be inferred by subtraction (80 and 106).

reporting_issues.issue: The number of people tested and randomized, and how many were excluded for salivary caffeine above the cut-offs or incomplete data, are not reported; the paper refers to Rogers et al. (2010) for details.
reporting_issues.consequence: Attrition and its possible link to treatment or consumer group cannot be assessed from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The Procedure gives the lunch time as 12:50 AM; from the schedule it must be 12:50 PM, five minutes after the second capsule.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; lunch shortly after the second dose was the same for all groups.

reporting_issues.issue: In Figure 1e (choice reaction time) the bar for non-low consumers on placebo carries no letter, so its pairwise comparisons with the other groups are not shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the comparison of that group with medium-high consumers on placebo cannot be read from the figure.

design_detail: Umbrella review (systematic review of meta-analyses) of coffee consumption and any health outcome in adults. PubMed, Embase, CINAHL and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews were searched from inception to July 2017, with reference lists; 141 articles gave 201 meta-analyses of observational studies (67 outcomes) and 17 meta-analyses of randomized trials (9 outcomes). Each meta-analysis with usable data was re-run with DerSimonian–Laird random effects (dose–response meta-analyses were taken as published); for each outcome and exposure contrast (high vs low or none, any vs none, one extra cup a day) one meta-analysis was chosen for the summary plots (the most recent; cohort subanalyses preferred); quality was scored with the original 11-item AMSTAR and certainty with GRADE. Primary studies were not reviewed.
can_establish: What the published meta-analyses up to July 2017 reported about coffee and each health outcome, re-expressed on a common random-effects basis, and how the authors graded the certainty of each body of evidence (about 75% very low, 25% low).
cannot_establish: Whether coffee causes any of the associations (almost all the evidence is observational, and the Mendelian randomization studies the authors cite found no genetic evidence of causation for type 2 diabetes or all-cause and cardiovascular mortality); absolute risks (none are given); the effect of a particular amount, preparation or caffeine content; the accuracy of the underlying primary studies, which were not reviewed; or effects that are not disease outcomes, such as heart rate, anxiety or sleep, which were outside its scope.

sample.recruitment: Database search with (coffee OR caffeine) AND (systematic review OR meta-analysis), inception to July 2017, plus manual searching of the reference lists of eligible articles (4 added) (pp. 2, 4).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: meta-analyses done with systematic methods, of cohort, case-control, cross-sectional (binary outcomes) or randomized studies, pooling relative risks, odds ratios, rate ratios or hazard ratios for coffee (total, caffeinated or decaffeinated) and any health outcome in adults of any population, setting or country; healthy or ill, pregnant or not, habitual or non-habitual drinkers (p. 2). Excluded at full text (126): reviews without meta-analysis 49, caffeine rather than coffee 33, conference abstracts 10, wrong exposure or design 5, coffee data not meta-analysed 5, duplicates 21, not in English 2, letter 1; and studies of genetic polymorphisms of coffee metabolism (pp. 2, 4).
sample.demographics: Mostly general-population cohorts; only one included meta-analysis concerned people with established disease (two small cohorts after myocardial infarction) (p. 14). Events and totals per meta-analysis are given in Figures 2–5; populations and exposure definitions are in appendices not read.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Re-analysis was possible for 83% of high-versus-low and 79% of any-versus-none comparisons and for none of the one-extra-cup (dose–response) estimates (p. 9).
sample.selection_effects: Only published meta-analyses were eligible, so outcomes never meta-analysed are missed (the authors name respiratory outcomes and sleep, p. 14); two non-English articles were excluded without a stated reason; no grey literature or registry search. One meta-analysis per outcome and contrast was plotted, chosen by recency, then number of cohort studies, then AMSTAR score (p. 3), so the plotted estimate is not necessarily the most valid. Several outcomes draw on the same original cohorts (p. 13).

exposure.measurement: As defined in each meta-analysis: mostly self-reported cups a day, with times, servings, millilitres, cups a week or month, or drinkers versus non-drinkers in some primary studies; there is no standard cup size, and bean, roast and brewing vary (p. 14). Contrasts: high versus low (or none), any versus none, and one extra cup a day (p. 3).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not standardized: the cups a day classed as high and low vary between primary studies (p. 14). Randomized-trial meta-analyses: blood pressure 1466 participants, mean 62 days, 2 to ≥5 cups; lipids mean 45 days, 2.4–8.0 cups; pregnancy one trial of 140 days at 3 cups (Figures 6–9, pp. 6–8).
exposure.polysubstance: Smoking is the confounder the authors discuss most: it goes with coffee drinking and with many outcomes; in the lung-cancer meta-analysis, the association disappeared in never smokers and in smoking-adjusted studies (pp. 8, 11). Age, BMI, alcohol, income, education and deprivation are named as further possible confounders (p. 13).

comparison.controls: Within each meta-analysis: low or no coffee consumption, or per-cup trends; in randomized trials, control arms without coffee.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level; adjustment varied between primary studies and was not reviewed.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The authors name residual confounding (smoking, age, BMI, alcohol, income, education, deprivation) and reverse causation, in which people cut down on coffee because of early symptoms of disease (pp. 13–14).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Smoking differs between coffee drinkers and non-drinkers; how far each primary study adjusted for it was not reviewed.

outcomes.instruments: Any health outcome reported in a meta-analysis: mortality (all-cause, cardiovascular, cancer), incident disease (cardiovascular, cancers, type 2 diabetes, liver, neurological, renal, musculoskeletal, gynaecological), pregnancy outcomes, and in randomized trials blood pressure, lipids and birth outcomes. Appraisal: original AMSTAR (11 points; meta-analyses using fixed effects downgraded) and GRADE for each outcome (p. 3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Median AMSTAR 5 of 11 (range 2–9, IQR 5–7); GRADE about 25% low and 75% very low, the randomized-trial meta-analyses included (rated low) (p. 10). AMSTAR and GRADE details are in appendices 3 and 4, not read.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Benefit' or 'harm' = a summary relative risk or odds ratio below or above 1 with a 95% interval excluding 1. 'Largest relative risk reduction at three to four cups a day' = the lowest point of non-linear dose–response curves in the included meta-analyses, taken as published.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: 67 observational and 9 randomized-trial outcomes across three exposure contrasts, each judged at p<0.05 (Egger's test at p<0.1).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Two reviewers screened titles and abstracts, reviewed full texts and extracted data independently, with a third arbitrating (pp. 2–3).

analysis.effect_sizes: Summary relative risks (or odds ratios where the source used them) with 95% intervals, τ², I² and Egger's P per outcome (Figures 2–5); mean differences for randomized trials (Figures 6, 7, 9). Main estimates: all-cause mortality lowest at three cups a day, 0.83 (0.79 to 0.88; corrected in BMJ 2018;360:k194, misprinted as 0.83 to 0.88), seven cups 0.90 (0.85 to 0.96), one extra cup 0.96 (0.94 to 0.97); cardiovascular mortality 0.81 (0.72 to 0.90); incident cardiovascular disease 0.85 (0.80 to 0.90); incident cancer 0.82 (0.74 to 0.89) high vs low; type 2 diabetes 0.70 (0.65 to 0.75) high vs low; chronic liver disease 0.35 (0.22 to 0.56) high vs low; liver cancer 0.50 (0.43 to 0.58) high vs low; Parkinson's disease 0.64 (0.53 to 0.76) high vs low; pregnancy: low birth weight OR 1.31 (1.03 to 1.67), pregnancy loss 1.46 (1.06 to 1.99); childhood acute leukaemia OR 1.57 (1.16 to 2.11); fracture in women 1.14 (1.05 to 1.24) vs men 0.76 (0.62 to 0.94). Randomized trials: total cholesterol +7.36 mg/dL (3.85 to 10.87), systolic blood pressure −0.66 mmHg (−2.71 to 1.39). About 40% of the 83 re-analysed meta-analyses had significant heterogeneity, 90% of these with I² above 50% (p. 9). No absolute risks and no prediction intervals.
analysis.covariates: As adjusted in the primary studies, which were not reviewed; cohort subanalyses were preferred to case-control or mixed estimates (p. 3).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the transparency statement says any discrepancies from the study as planned have been explained (p. 15).
analysis.selective_reporting: The summary plots show only the 10 most harmful and 10 most beneficial associations per contrast (Figures 2–4), with full plots in appendix 1 (not read). The plotted meta-analysis per outcome was chosen by recency rather than quality (p. 3). Dose–response results, including the three-to-four-cup minimum, were taken from the source meta-analyses without re-analysis (p. 3).
analysis.power: Not applicable at review level; many estimates rest on 2–3 studies, and the authors note that meta-analyses of decaffeinated coffee had much lower power (p. 12).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 218 published meta-analyses, almost all of observational studies and rated low or very low certainty by the authors' own GRADE, coffee drinking was more often associated with lower than with higher risk: all-cause mortality RR 0.83 (0.79 to 0.88, as corrected in BMJ 2018;360:k194) at about three cups a day versus none, cardiovascular mortality 0.81, incident cancer 0.82 (high vs low), and the largest associations for liver disease (chronic liver disease 0.35 high vs low). Harmful associations: pregnancy outcomes (low birth weight OR 1.31, pregnancy loss 1.46, each from a single meta-analysis), childhood leukaemia (case-control evidence only), fracture in women (1.14, against 0.76 in men), and lung cancer, which disappeared in never smokers. In randomized trials coffee raised total cholesterol by about 0.19 mmol/L, more with unfiltered than with filtered coffee, and did not change blood pressure.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that coffee "seems generally safe within usual levels of intake" and is more likely to benefit health than harm, with the largest risk reduction at three to four cups a day (p. 1). Gaps: (1) the evidence is associational and the authors' own GRADE rates it low or very low (p. 10), which the abstract does not state (the summary box calls the evidence observational and of lower quality); the Mendelian randomization studies they cite found no genetic evidence that coffee causes the lower risk of type 2 diabetes or of all-cause and cardiovascular mortality (p. 13), which the abstract does not mention, though it does say randomized trials are needed to establish causation; (2) three to four cups is where observational dose–response curves bottomed out, taken as published without re-analysis (p. 3), not an amount tested in people, yet the conclusions suggest future trials might be optimised at that level (p. 14); (3) 'safe' means no consistent harmful association with disease outcomes in published meta-analyses, while physiological effects such as heart rate, anxiety and sleep were outside the review (p. 14), and studies of genetic differences in caffeine metabolism were excluded (p. 2), although the authors cite one in which the hypertension risk was higher with slow-metabolism CYP1A2 alleles (p. 14); (4) the abstract says harmful associations were largely nullified by adjustment for smoking except in pregnancy, but the paper shows this only for lung cancer and, through smoker and non-smoker strata, cancer mortality (pp. 8, 11); (5) eight numerical errors, including the abstract's all-cause mortality interval, were corrected in BMJ 2018;360:k194 (all-cause mortality 0.83, 0.79 to 0.88); the correction says they do not affect the findings, which holds for the direction of the associations, but the corrected any-versus-none cirrhosis estimate (0.89, 0.73 to 1.08) includes 1, so of the three cirrhosis contrasts only the per-cup estimate (0.77, 0.64 to 0.87) excludes it; (6) no absolute risks are given. Rated substantial rather than minor (adjudication, 12 November 2026): the abstract's headline conclusion states benefit and safety that rest on associations the authors themselves grade low or very low, without the null genetic evidence and with a smoking explanation generalized from two outcomes; only the body's Conclusions are cautious (p. 14). A headline 'three to four cups a day makes you live longer' overstates the paper. A fair summary: in observational studies, coffee drinkers had somewhat lower risks of death and of several diseases, with pregnancy and fracture in women as the exceptions, and whether coffee is the reason is unknown.

timeline.event: Ding et al. dose–response meta-analysis of prospective cohorts on coffee and cardiovascular disease (ref. 19): incident cardiovascular disease 0.85 (0.80 to 0.90), lowest at three to five cups a day, as summarized here (p. 7).

Nordestgaard & Nordestgaard (and Nordestgaard et al., 2015): Mendelian randomization analyses found no genetic evidence of a causal relation of coffee with type 2 diabetes or with all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, as described by Poole et al. (p. 13; refs 122–123).

Grosso et al. dose–response meta-analysis in smokers and non-smokers (ref. 28): source of the all-cause and cardiovascular mortality estimates; in smokers, cancer mortality rose with coffee at all levels (pp. 6–8, 11).

Gunter et al. (10 European countries, 521 330 people) and Park et al. (185 855 people): cohort studies with lower all-cause mortality among coffee drinkers, described by the authors as agreeing with this review (p. 13).
This umbrella review.

Correction notice (BMJ 2018;360:k194, published 12 January 2018; read with this article): eight numerical errors corrected, among them the all-cause mortality interval (0.83, 0.79 to 0.88), decaffeinated all-cause mortality (0.89, 0.85 to 0.93), stroke mortality (0.70, 0.57 to 0.86), cirrhosis any versus none (0.89, 0.73 to 1.08) and per extra cup (0.77, 0.64 to 0.87), lung cancer high versus low in the text (1.56, 1.12 to 2.17), fracture per cup in women in the Discussion (5%) and all-cause mortality in women in a European cohort (0.93, 0.87 to 0.98); the authors state that the errors do not affect their findings, and appendices 1 and 2 were revised.

replication.where_it_stands: A map of meta-analyses published up to July 2017, not new data; its estimates depend on the included meta-analyses being accurate, which the authors did not check against the primary studies. The observational associations are consistent across many outcomes, but the genetic studies the authors cite did not support causation for diabetes or mortality, so whether coffee itself lowers risk remains open. The project's caffeine list holds later Mendelian randomization work (for example Yuan et al., 2021; Pham et al., 2025) and the Crippa et al. (2014) mortality meta-analysis with its published critique (Aubin, 2015), none read for this card.

funding.funder: No specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors; the authors state they remain independent of any funding influence (p. 15).
funding.declared_conflicts: All authors declare no support from any organisation for the submitted work. Fallowfield reports research grants from GlaxoSmithKline and Intercept Pharmaceuticals and personal fees from Novartis and Merck; Hayes reports personal fees from MSD, Gilead, Abbvie, Janssen (printed 'Jannsen'), BMS, Pfizer and Novartis, and grants and personal fees from Roche; all outside the submitted work (p. 15).
funding.affiliations_note: The review includes two meta-analyses by its own authors (cirrhosis, ref. 9; hepatocellular carcinoma, ref. 10), which carry the highest AMSTAR scores in the summary plots (9 and 8; Figures 4 and 5), and its patient-involvement work was aimed at a future trial of coffee in chronic liver disease (p. 3). Of the included meta-analyses, one declared support from an organisation linked to the coffee industry and another's authors contributed to the same organisation; neither was plotted (p. 14). Funding of primary studies was not reviewed. Recorded as flags, not as reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Long-term randomized trials of coffee versus no coffee with patient-important outcomes, starting where the observational signal is strongest (chronic liver disease), together with Mendelian randomization analyses that allow for non-linear effects and individual-participant analyses of cohorts with harmonized exposure definitions, stratified by smoking and reporting absolute risks.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Adults; coffee (total, caffeinated, decaffeinated); three exposure contrasts; any health outcome (pp. 2–3).

domains.domain: 2. Protocol registered before the review (critical)
domains.note: No protocol or registration is reported.

domains.domain: 3. Explanation of study designs included
domains.note: Meta-analyses only, with reasons; cohort subanalyses preferred to case-control because of recall and selection bias and reverse causation (pp. 2–3).

domains.domain: 4. Comprehensive literature search (critical)
domains.note: Four databases, search terms given, reference lists searched and the search run about three months before acceptance; but two non-English articles were excluded without a stated reason (which fails the partial-yes criterion of justified publication restrictions), and there was no grey-literature, registry or expert search. Otherwise a reasonable search for an umbrella review; a close call.

domains.domain: 5. Study selection in duplicate
domains.note: Two reviewers screened titles, abstracts and full texts independently, with a third arbitrating (p. 2).

domains.domain: 6. Data extraction in duplicate
domains.note: Two reviewers extracted independently; differences resolved by consensus (pp. 2–3).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Reasons for the 126 full-text exclusions are given only as counts in the flowchart (p. 4); no list of excluded articles, and the appendices listed on the unnumbered last page (PDF p. 18) do not include one.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Per outcome: events and totals, follow-up range, number and design of studies, τ², I², Egger's P and AMSTAR score (Figures 2–5); populations, exposure categories and settings only in appendices (not read).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: The included meta-analyses were scored with the original AMSTAR, which the authors note gives primary-study quality only 2 of 11 points (p. 12), and each outcome was graded with GRADE (details in appendix 4, not read); risk of bias in the primary studies (confounding, selection) was not assessed directly.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Funding of the included meta-analyses was extracted but reported only as a summary of coffee-industry links; funding of primary studies was not reviewed (p. 14).

domains.domain: 11. Appropriate statistical methods for meta-analysis (critical)
domains.note: Re-analysis with DerSimonian–Laird random effects on the log scale with τ² and I²; dose–response meta-analyses taken as published; mixing of odds ratios, rate ratios and hazard ratios inside included meta-analyses accepted without adjustment (p. 12). Judged met on balance for an umbrella review that re-runs rather than pools across meta-analyses.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No analysis of how study quality affects the estimates; AMSTAR was used only as a tie-breaker when choosing which meta-analysis to plot (p. 3).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The discussion and conclusions stress observational design, residual confounding, reverse causation and low or very low GRADE certainty (pp. 12–14).

domains.domain: 14. Heterogeneity explained and discussed
domains.note: τ² and I² given per estimate; about 40% of the 83 re-analysed meta-analyses had significant heterogeneity, discussed with its likely sources (population, coffee type, exposure measurement, follow-up) and with effect modification by sex for fracture and by smoking (pp. 9, 11).

domains.domain: 15. Publication bias investigated (critical)
domains.note: Egger's test for re-analyses with at least 10 studies (40% of re-analyses), 20% of which showed small-study effects; the authors say unmeasured publication bias may affect many estimates (pp. 3, 10).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and each author's interests declared (p. 15).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Three critical items are not met (no protocol; no list of excluded articles; a search with an unexplained language restriction and no grey literature), which under AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence; item 9 is only partly met because primary-study risk of bias was not assessed. The rating concerns the umbrella review as a synthesis; it does not change the individual meta-analyses' estimates, which the review re-expresses without checking them against primary studies. Cite it as a map of what published meta-analyses reported up to 2017 and of the authors' certainty ratings (mostly very low), not as evidence that coffee causes any outcome. Take specific estimates from the underlying meta-analyses where possible, and use the values corrected in BMJ 2018;360:k194 (all-cause, decaffeinated all-cause and stroke mortality, cirrhosis, lung cancer, fracture in women and the European cohort), not the printed ones.

key_findings.finding: Scope: 201 meta-analyses of observational research covering 67 outcomes and 17 meta-analyses of randomized trials covering 9 outcomes, from 141 articles; median 2 meta-analyses per observational outcome (IQR 1–4, range 1–11), and 22 outcomes had only one. The randomized-trial outcomes were limited to blood pressure, lipids and three pregnancy outcomes.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 3, continuing on p. 4); Figure 1 (p. 4)
key_findings.note: 'Twenty two' outcomes is spelled out in the text.

key_findings.finding: Certainty: the authors graded the evidence for about 75% of outcomes as very low and about 25% as low (GRADE), the randomized-trial meta-analyses included; the included meta-analyses had a median AMSTAR score of 5 of 11 (range 2–9, IQR 5–7).
key_findings.locator: Results › AMSTAR and GRADE classification of included studies

key_findings.finding: All-cause mortality (Grosso et al.): relative risk lowest at three cups a day versus none, 0.83 (0.79 to 0.88), corrected in BMJ 2018;360:k194 (the abstract and Results had misprinted the interval as 0.83 to 0.88); at seven cups 0.90 (0.85 to 0.96). A separate linear analysis gave 0.96 (0.94 to 0.97) per extra cup despite significant non-linearity (P<0.001).
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 1); Results › All cause mortality, 1st paragraph (p. 6); correction notice BMJ 2018;360:k194
key_findings.note: The printed interval put the estimate on its own lower bound; the correction notice, read with the paper, gives 0.79 to 0.88 and states that its corrections do not affect the authors' findings.

key_findings.finding: Cardiovascular mortality was lowest at three cups a day versus none: 0.81 (0.72 to 0.90); coronary heart disease mortality 0.84 (0.71 to 0.99); stroke mortality 0.70 (0.57 to 0.86), corrected in BMJ 2018;360:k194 (interval misprinted as 0.80 to 0.90). Above three cups the associations weakened without turning harmful. Incident cardiovascular disease 0.85 (0.80 to 0.90), coronary heart disease 0.90 (0.84 to 0.97) and stroke 0.80 (0.75 to 0.86), lowest at three to five cups a day.
key_findings.locator: Results › Cardiovascular disease, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; correction notice BMJ 2018;360:k194
key_findings.note: The printed stroke-mortality interval excluded its own estimate; the correction notice gives 0.57 to 0.86.

key_findings.finding: Cancer: in a meta-analysis of 40 cohort studies, incident cancer was 0.82 (0.74 to 0.89) for high versus low consumption, 0.87 (0.82 to 0.92) any versus none and 0.97 (0.96 to 0.98) per extra cup. In non-smokers, cancer mortality was 0.98 (0.96 to 1.00) per extra cup; in smokers it rose with coffee at all levels, significantly above four cups a day.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 1); Results › Cancer, 1st paragraph (p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Liver outcomes had the largest associations: chronic liver disease 0.35 (0.22 to 0.56) high versus low, 0.62 (0.47 to 0.82) any versus none and 0.74 (0.65 to 0.83) per extra cup; liver cancer 0.50 (0.43 to 0.58) high versus low; non-alcoholic fatty liver disease 0.71 (0.60 to 0.85) any versus none (3 studies, including cross-sectional ones). Cirrhosis: any versus none 0.89 (0.73 to 1.08) in the authors' cohort re-analysis and per extra cup 0.77 (0.64 to 0.87), both corrected in BMJ 2018;360:k194 (misprinted as 0.61, 0.45 to 0.84, and 0.83, 0.78 to 0.88); high versus low 0.69 (0.44 to 1.07). The authors note that only the high-versus-low associations for liver cancer and chronic liver disease reached the size (below 0.5 or above 2) that can allow GRADE upgrading.
key_findings.locator: Figure 2 (p. 4); Figures 3 and 4 (p. 5); Results › Liver and gastrointestinal outcomes, 1st paragraph (pp. 8–9); Discussion › Strengths and weaknesses, 4th paragraph (p. 12); correction notice BMJ 2018;360:k194
key_findings.note: The misprinted any-versus-none value was the source paper's pooled estimate from 3 cohort and 4 case-control studies, which put cirrhosis among the 10 most beneficial associations of Figure 3; the per-cup value had been converted from a two-cup estimate by a cube root instead of a square root. The text (p. 8) prints the same two values; the correction names the text for the first and Figure 4 for the second.

key_findings.finding: Type 2 diabetes 0.70 (0.65 to 0.75) high versus low and 0.94 (0.93 to 0.95) per extra cup; Parkinson's disease 0.64 (0.53 to 0.76) high versus low, consistent after adjustment for smoking; depression 0.92 (0.87 to 0.97) per extra cup (5 studies, including cross-sectional ones).
key_findings.locator: Figure 2 (p. 4); Figure 4 (p. 5); Results › Metabolic disease, 1st paragraph; Neurological outcomes (p. 9)

key_findings.finding: Pregnancy outcomes were, with fracture in women, the exceptions the authors name to the absence of consistent harmful associations; they find 'some consistency' for pregnancy, each outcome resting on a single meta-analysis (partly subgroups of reviews of total caffeine): high versus low consumption was associated with low birth weight, OR 1.31 (1.03 to 1.67; 2 cohort studies), pregnancy loss 1.46 (1.06 to 1.99; 5 cohort studies, I² 87%), and preterm birth in the first (1.22, 1.00 to 1.49) and second trimester (1.12, 1.02 to 1.22). The only randomized trial (one study, 1153 participants) showed no significant effect on preterm birth (0.81, 0.48 to 1.37).
key_findings.locator: Figure 2 (p. 4); Figure 8 (p. 7); Results › Antenatal exposure to coffee, 1st paragraph (p. 9); Discussion › Principal findings and possible explanations, 3rd paragraph (p. 10)

key_findings.finding: Coffee in pregnancy was associated with childhood acute leukaemia, OR 1.57 (1.16 to 2.11) high versus low and 1.44 (1.07 to 1.92) any versus none, with the evidence coming from case-control studies.
key_findings.locator: Results › Antenatal exposure to coffee, 2nd paragraph (p. 9); Discussion › Principal findings and possible explanations, 3rd paragraph (p. 10)

key_findings.finding: Fracture risk differed by sex: high versus low consumption 1.14 (1.05 to 1.24) in women and 0.76 (0.62 to 0.94) in men (ratio 1.50, 1.20 to 1.88; P<0.001); per extra cup 1.05 (1.02 to 1.07) in women and 0.91 (0.87 to 0.95) in men; no significant association overall. The authors note that many fracture studies did not adjust for BMI, smoking, calcium, vitamin D or alcohol.
key_findings.locator: Results › Musculoskeletal outcomes (p. 9); Discussion › Principal findings and possible explanations, 4th paragraph (starting p. 10, continuing on p. 11)

key_findings.finding: Lung cancer was associated with coffee (high versus low OR 1.56, 1.12 to 2.17, the authors' re-analysis of 5 cohort studies in Figure 2, corrected in BMJ 2018;360:k194 for the text, which had printed the source paper's 1.59, 1.26 to 2.00; any versus none 1.28, 1.12 to 1.47; per extra cup 1.04, 1.03 to 1.05), but in people who had never smoked the any-versus-none estimate was 0.92 (0.75 to 1.10) and in smoking-adjusted studies 1.03 (0.95 to 1.12); the authors judge it likely that residual confounding by smoking, despite some adjustment, can explain the association.
key_findings.locator: Figure 2 (p. 4); Results › Cancer, 3rd paragraph (p. 8); Discussion › Principal findings and possible explanations, 5th paragraph (p. 11); correction notice BMJ 2018;360:k194

key_findings.finding: Randomized trials: coffee raised total cholesterol by 7.36 mg/dL (3.85 to 10.87), or 0.19 mmol/L (12 trials, 1017 participants, mean 45 days, 2.4–8.0 cups a day), with larger rises for unfiltered coffee (12.90 mg/dL) than filtered (3.60 mg/dL); the blood-pressure differences were not significant, systolic −0.66 mmHg (−2.71 to 1.39), diastolic −0.45 (−1.51 to 0.61) (12 trials, 1466 participants, mean 62 days), described by the authors as a marginally beneficial association that did not reach significance.
key_findings.locator: Figure 6 (p. 6); Figure 7 (p. 7); Results › Cardiovascular disease, 3rd paragraph (p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Decaffeinated coffee: the authors report lower all-cause mortality with higher intake, lowest at three cups a day, 0.89 (0.85 to 0.93), corrected in BMJ 2018;360:k194 (misprinted as 0.83, 0.85 to 0.89); at the maximum consumption of the same non-linear analysis Figure 5 gives 0.90 (0.79 to 1.01; 5 cohort studies), not significant. Per extra cup, type 2 diabetes 0.94 (0.91 to 0.98) and endometrial cancer 0.96 (0.92 to 0.99); the authors found no convincing harmful association with decaffeinated coffee.
key_findings.locator: Figure 5 (p. 6); Results › All cause mortality, 1st paragraph (continuing on p. 7); Discussion › Principal findings and possible explanations, 9th paragraph (p. 12); correction notice BMJ 2018;360:k194
key_findings.note: The correction changes the estimate itself, not only the interval: an 11% rather than 17% lower relative risk (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: The authors report that Mendelian randomization studies found no genetic evidence of a causal relation between coffee and lower risk of type 2 diabetes or of all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, suggesting residual confounding, while noting that these analyses assume a linear relation; they name smoking, age, BMI, alcohol, income, education and deprivation as possible confounders. They also cite one genetic study (Palatini et al.) in which the coffee-associated risk of hypertension was higher with CYP1A2 alleles for slow than for fast caffeine metabolism; studies of genetic polymorphisms for coffee metabolism were excluded from the review.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Eligibility criteria and data extraction (p. 2); Discussion › Strengths and weaknesses and in relation to other studies, 9th paragraph (p. 13, right column, continuing on p. 14)

key_findings.finding: Heterogeneity and small-study bias: about 40% of the 83 re-analysed meta-analyses had significant heterogeneity, 90% of these with I² above 50%; Egger's test could be run on 40% of re-analyses and showed small-study effects in 20% of those, for example type 2 diabetes (P=0.049), endometrial cancer (P=0.03), hip fracture (P=0.02) and the randomized-trial total cholesterol estimate (P<0.01).
key_findings.locator: Results › Heterogeneity of included studies (p. 9); Publication bias of included studies (p. 10)

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: primary studies were not reviewed, dose–response meta-analyses were not re-run, the included meta-analyses were assumed to report their data accurately, several outcomes share the same original cohorts, and physiological effects such as heart rate, stimulation and anxiety were outside the review; only one included meta-analysis concerned people with established disease (two small cohorts after myocardial infarction).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Method of analysis (p. 3); Discussion › Strengths and weaknesses, 5th and 6th paragraphs (p. 13); 12th and 13th paragraphs (p. 14)

key_findings.finding: Industry links among included meta-analyses: one declared support from an organisation linked to the coffee industry and in another the authors had contributed to the same organisation; neither was selected for the summary plots, and the funding of primary studies was not reviewed.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Strengths and weaknesses and in relation to other studies, 14th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The all-cause mortality estimate at three cups a day was printed as 0.83 (0.83 to 0.88) in the abstract and in the Results, the point estimate on the lower bound of its own interval; the correction notice gives 0.83 (0.79 to 0.88).
reporting_issues.consequence: Misprint, corrected in BMJ 2018;360:k194; cite 0.83 (0.79 to 0.88).

reporting_issues.issue: The decaffeinated-coffee all-cause mortality estimate at three cups a day was printed as 0.83 (0.85 to 0.89), the point estimate outside its interval; the correction notice gives 0.89 (0.85 to 0.93).
reporting_issues.consequence: The estimate itself was misprinted (an 11% rather than 17% lower relative risk, editors' arithmetic); corrected in BMJ 2018;360:k194.

reporting_issues.issue: Stroke mortality at three cups a day was printed as 30% lower, 0.70 (0.80 to 0.90), the point estimate outside its interval; the correction notice gives 0.70 (0.57 to 0.86).
reporting_issues.consequence: The interval was misprinted and the 30% figure stands; corrected in BMJ 2018;360:k194.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the randomized-trial change in HDL cholesterol as −0.002 mmol/L with an interval from −0.02 mmol/L to '0.54 mol/L', while Figure 7 gives −0.11 mg/dL (−0.76 to 0.54); the upper bound was left in mg/dL with the wrong unit.
reporting_issues.consequence: Unit and conversion error; editors' arithmetic with the paper's factor (38.6 mg/dL per mmol/L) gives about −0.003 (−0.02 to 0.01) mmol/L, a null result either way.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results give the fracture risk per extra cup in women as 1.05 (1.02 to 1.07), but the Discussion described it as a 0.6% increased risk; the correction notice changes the Discussion figure to 5%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Misprint in the Discussion, corrected in BMJ 2018;360:k194; the Results value stands.

reporting_issues.issue: Lung cancer, high versus low consumption, from the same meta-analysis (ref. 46): Figure 2 gives 1.56 (1.12 to 2.17) for 5 cohort studies, the text printed an odds ratio of 1.59 (1.26 to 2.00); the correction notice states that the text value came from the original paper rather than the authors' re-analysis and should read 1.56 (1.12 to 2.17).
reporting_issues.consequence: Corrected in BMJ 2018;360:k194; cite 1.56 (1.12 to 2.17), the authors' re-analysis.

reporting_issues.issue: In Figure 5 (decaffeinated coffee), the type 2 diabetes per-cup row lists 14 studies in total but 16 cohort studies, and the liver cancer row lists 3 studies with 0 cohort and 0 case-control studies.
reporting_issues.consequence: Study counts in the decaffeinated-coffee figure cannot be relied on.

reporting_issues.issue: Two intervals are strongly lopsided on the log scale: hip fracture in men 0.53 (0.38 to 1.00) (p. 9) and all-cause mortality in women in a European cohort, printed as 0.93 (0.82 to 0.95) (p. 13).
reporting_issues.consequence: The European-cohort interval was a misprint, corrected in BMJ 2018;360:k194 to 0.93 (0.87 to 0.98). The hip-fracture interval was not corrected, and the printed interaction test (2.40, 1.35 to 4.24) reproduces from it (editors' arithmetic), so it is probably as in the source meta-analysis, which should be checked before it is cited; lopsidedness alone does not mark a misprint here (the corrected per-cup cirrhosis interval, 0.77 with 0.64 to 0.87, is lopsided too).

reporting_issues.issue: Two cirrhosis estimates were wrong as printed: any versus none, Figure 3 and the text gave 0.61 (0.45 to 0.84), labelled as 3 cohort studies and as the authors' re-analysis, but it was the source paper's estimate from 3 cohort and 4 case-control studies; per extra cup, Figure 4 and the text gave 0.83 (0.78 to 0.88) after a two-cup estimate had been converted by a cube root instead of a square root.
reporting_issues.consequence: Corrected in BMJ 2018;360:k194 to 0.89 (0.73 to 1.08), which takes cirrhosis out of the 10 most beneficial associations of Figure 3, and to 0.77 (0.64 to 0.87), which does not change its rank in Figure 4; the correction also revised online appendices 1 and 2.

design_detail: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group laboratory study on one test day (Department of Experimental Psychology, University of Bristol, UK), with two observational factors: habitual caffeine consumption (self-selected; nonconsumer N, low L, medium M and high H groups, or non-/low NL under 40 mg/day vs medium/high MH 40 mg/day or more) and genotype at 8 ADORA2A and 9 ADORA1 single nucleotide polymorphisms (candidate-gene association). After abstaining from caffeine and alcohol from 19:00 the previous evening, 416 adults were randomized, stratified by interview-reported intake and age, to caffeine capsules (100 mg at 11:15 and 150 mg at 12:45) or placebo at both times. Anxiety, alertness and headache were self-rated (MAPSS, 0–8) at baseline (10:30) and in three post-treatment sessions (12:00, 13:45, 15:00). 379 were analysed (162 NL, 217 MH). Treatment was randomized; consumer group and genotype were not. The companion report on performance and alertness (Rogers et al., 2013; sc_rogers_2013) comes from the same protocol and test day.
can_establish: The acute effect of 100 mg plus 150 mg of caffeine against placebo on self-rated anxiety, alertness and headache after about 16 hours without caffeine, within groups defined by habitual intake and by ADORA2A genotype (randomized comparisons), and whether genotype frequencies differ between habitual-intake groups (association).
cannot_establish: That differences between habitual-intake groups were caused by tolerance or by withdrawal (consumer groups were self-selected, not randomized), that caffeine gives no net benefit for alertness (no test against nonconsumers on placebo is reported), or effects of other amounts, schedules or everyday patterns of consumption.

sample.recruitment: 44% from respondents to a postal survey of caffeine habits and health done the previous year, provisionally grouped by intake (under 40 vs at least 40 mg/day) and age (under 30 vs at least 30 years) and selected at random within these groups to give similar numbers of infrequent and frequent consumers of similar ages, although only 10% of that population took under 40 mg/day; the rest through local advertisements and word of mouth targeting infrequent and frequent consumers. Suitability assessed by telephone or face-to-face interview. Presented to participants as a study of genetic variation, caffeine habits and caffeine effects; participants were paid 50 pounds (p. 1974; Table 1, p. 1975).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Inclusion: age 18–65; good general physical and mental health; available and willing to attend a 7-h session that might include caffeine; willing to give a blood sample for genotyping; nonsmoker or light smoker (5 cigarettes or equivalent a day or fewer); normal blood pressure; not pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding (p. 1974). Excluded after randomization on the baseline saliva sample (11:10, before the first capsule): non-/low consumers with caffeine and/or paraxanthine above 0.2 µg/ml (n=15) and medium/high consumers with caffeine above 2 µg/ml (n=5) (p. 1976).
sample.demographics: Analysed sample (Table 2, p. 1977), N/L/M/H: habitual intake 1.3 (SD 1.7), 19 (10), 128 (46) and 346 (129) mg/day; age 34.1 (13.3), 29.9 (11.2), 32.5 (12.4) and 35.4 (13.1) years (F(3, 375)=3.23, P=0.023); men/women 35/46, 39/42, 49/60 and 57/51; smokers 7, 13, 22 and 20 (smoking data missing for 4). Overall aged 18–62, 47% men, 16.5% smokers, 95% white European (p. 1976). Intake from 0 mg (43 participants) to 778 mg/day; 55 above 300 mg/day; lowest in the H group 203 mg/day (p. 1977). Education not reported.
sample.attrition: 416 randomized (218 women, 198 men; p. 1974). Removed (p. 1976): 4 without genetic data (DNA extraction problems); 15 non-/low and 5 medium/high consumers on baseline saliva; 8 who withdrew after at least the first capsule (5 medium/high consumers, all on placebo, 4 citing headache and feeling sick and 1 no reason; 3 non-/low consumers, 2 on caffeine and 1 on placebo, no reasons given); 5 with missing data from equipment malfunction. 379 analysed. The 33 removed for saliva, withdrawal or missing data did not differ in rs5751876 genotype from the 379 (chi-squared 0.05, df 2). Editors' comparison: the 2013 report from this protocol analysed 369 (157 NL, 212 MH, as recorded on sc_rogers_2013), 5 fewer in each group; the reason is not given in this paper.
sample.selection_effects: Infrequent consumers were deliberately over-sampled: they make up 43% of the analysed sample (editors' arithmetic, 162 of 379) against 10% of the survey population (p. 1974). Consumer groups are self-selected. Volunteers had to be willing to take caffeine and give blood; the sample is 95% white European with no or light smoking. The analysis set excludes those who withdrew, and all withdrawals among medium/high consumers were on placebo with headache or sickness as the usual reason. The authors check for under-recruitment of anxiety-prone people: TT frequencies close to Hardy–Weinberg expectations in both consumer groups, and fewer than 2% of contacted infrequent consumers who did not take part cited concern about caffeine's effects (p. 1982).

exposure.measurement: Habitual intake from a questionnaire completed in the week before testing (frequency of teas, coffees, colas, other caffeine-containing drinks and products, chocolate), converted to mg/day with dietary and manufacturers' values (for example instant coffee 54 mg, ground coffee 105 mg, tea 40 mg) and analysed after the participant had been tested (p. 1974). Abstinence checked by salivary caffeine and paraxanthine at 11:10 (HPLC, limit of detection 0.02 µg/ml; pp. 1975–1976). Treatment: caffeine BP anhydrous powder or cornflour placebo in identical white size-1 capsules, double-blind (p. 1975). Genotypes by TaqMan or RFLP assays, assigned blind to group and phenotype; about 10% (n=45) re-genotyped with 100% concordance (p. 1976).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: 100 mg caffeine by mouth at 11:15 and 150 mg at 12:45, or placebo at both times, after abstaining from caffeine from 19:00 the previous evening (16 h before the first capsule, as the abstract states); lunch (580–740 kcal) after the second capsule; water available throughout (Table 1 and pp. 1974–1975). Salivary caffeine in the caffeine group 1.64 (SD 0.68) µg/ml 90 min after the first dose and 2.86 (SD 1.21) µg/ml 90 min after the second (p. 1977).
exposure.polysubstance: Light smoking (at most 5 cigarettes a day) allowed outside the test day; no smoking on the test day until leaving the laboratory; smoking used as a covariate for alertness because smokers were less alert (data not shown, p. 1977). Alcohol prohibited from 19:00 the previous evening. Other drug use not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Caffeine abstinence from 19:00 the previous evening, about 15.5 h at the start of the baseline session and 16 h at the first capsule (editors' arithmetic from Table 1, p. 1975); checked by saliva, with 20 participants excluded (p. 1976).

comparison.controls: For the caffeine effect: placebo within the same consumer and genotype group (randomized). For withdrawal and net benefit: nonconsumers (N) given placebo, used by the authors as the benchmark level of alertness (not randomized) (pp. 1974, 1977).
comparison.matching: None between consumer groups. Age as a covariate and gender as a factor in all analyses; smoking as an added covariate for alertness; baseline anxiety as a covariate in some analyses of anxiety (p. 1976).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measure of how anxious, alert or headache-prone people were before they became caffeine consumers; prior-night sleep, chronotype, personality and education not reported. The authors raise the alternative that frequent consumers are constitutionally less alert and argue against it, but do not test it (p. 1980).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Smoking only (Table 2, p. 1977); alcohol and other drugs not reported.

outcomes.instruments: MAPSS, 24 items (single descriptors or clusters, for example one on feeling mentally alert, attentive, able to concentrate and observant, one on feeling tense, anxious, nervous or on edge, and one on headache), rated 1–9 and rescaled 0–8; which items make up the anxiety, alertness and headache scores is given only in the online supplement (not read), and since Rogers et al. (2013, p. 231) say this report did not analyse sleepiness/wakefulness and mental alertness separately, its alertness score may combine the two.
outcomes.validity_norms: MAPSS was adapted from the authors' earlier instruments; full details are in an online supplement (not read); no validation data or norms in the paper.
outcomes.operationalization: Tolerance: a smaller caffeine–placebo difference in higher-intake groups. Withdrawal: lower alertness or more headache in higher-intake groups on placebo. No net benefit: caffeine not raising alertness above the level of nonconsumers on placebo. Genotype susceptibility: a caffeine by genotype interaction for anxiety.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Bonferroni across the 8 ADORA2A loci (alpha 0.00625) and 7 ADORA1 loci (alpha 0.00714); alpha 0.017 for the three comparisons of habitual intake by genotype; Bonferroni t-tests for caffeine against placebo within groups (p. 1976). No correction across the three ratings, the sessions or the alternative model specifications.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind with identical capsules (p. 1975); ratings self-reported on computer; genotypes assigned blind to group and phenotype (p. 1976). Participants knew they had abstained overnight.

analysis.effect_sizes: Analyses of variance; no standardized effect sizes or confidence intervals. Caffeine by consumer status (four groups): anxiety F(3, 362)=7.03, P=0.0001; alertness F(3, 362)=6.06, P=0.0005 (F(3, 357)=6.31, P=0.0004 with smoking); headache F(3, 362)=9.52, P<0.0001 (p. 1977). ADORA2A rs5751876, anxiety after 100 mg: caffeine by genotype F(2, 366)=2.72, P=0.067, and with baseline anxiety as covariate F(2, 365)=6.57, P=0.002 (pp. 1977, 1979); mean increase 0.67 points in TT against 0.11 in CC and CT (0–8 scale; p. 1981); for rs3761422 TT, caffeine 1.65 (SE 0.15) vs placebo 0.95 (SE 0.17) (p. 1978). Combined model: caffeine by genotype F(1, 361)=7.16, P=0.008, above the corrected threshold (p. 1978). Editors' reading of Figures 1 and 4 (approximate, 0–8 scale): anxiety on caffeine vs placebo about 1.2 vs 0.5 (N), 1.4 vs 0.7 (L), 0.9 vs 0.8 (M), 0.8 vs 1.0 (H); alertness about 4.8 vs 4.9 (N), 5.0 vs 4.7 (L), 5.1 vs 4.4 (M), 4.9 vs 3.7 (H); headache about 1.2 vs 0.7 (N), 1.2 vs 1.0 (L), 1.1 vs 1.1 (M), 0.9 vs 1.8 (H); anxiety in TT carriers about 1.76 vs 0.84 (NL) and 1.37 vs 1.00 (MH).
analysis.covariates: Age and gender in all analyses; smoking for alertness; baseline anxiety in some analyses of anxiety.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol reported. Primary hypotheses are stated in the Introduction: greater anxiety after caffeine in infrequent consumers and in rs5751876 TT carriers, and lower habitual intake in TT carriers; withdrawal reversal was a secondary objective (p. 1974). Target sample size 400 (p. 1974).
analysis.selective_reporting: Performance, attention, vigilance, hand steadiness, heart rate, blood pressure and taste were to be reported elsewhere (p. 1975). Several analyses are reported as data not shown (smoking, ADORA1 associations, rs3761422 combined analyses). The genotype by caffeine effect is significant in one of three specifications (session 1 with baseline covariate) and the paper leads with it.
analysis.power: Target sample 400 (p. 1974); no power calculation. Medium/high consumers with the TT genotype numbered 35 (p. 1978), and their split between caffeine and placebo is not reported; the authors call this a relatively small sample (p. 1978).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 379 adults after about 16 h without caffeine, 100 mg plus 150 mg of caffeine raised self-rated anxiety in nonconsumers and low consumers but not in medium or high consumers; on placebo, alertness was lower the higher the habitual intake, and caffeine kept medium and high consumers at about the level of nonconsumers on placebo; headache was higher on placebo in high consumers and higher on caffeine in nonconsumers. After 100 mg, anxiety rose more in rs5751876 TT carriers (0.67 vs 0.11 points on a 0–8 scale) in the analysis adjusted for baseline anxiety. Genotype frequencies did not differ between non-/low and medium/high consumers, and TT carriers among medium/high consumers took more caffeine from coffee.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that with frequent consumption "substantial tolerance develops to the anxiogenic effect of caffeine, even in genetically susceptible individuals" and that no net benefit for alertness is gained because abstinence lowers alertness and caffeine only restores it (p. 1973); the conclusion says frequent consumption is maintained by avoiding withdrawal (p. 1982). Gaps: tolerance and withdrawal are inferred from differences between self-selected consumer groups, not from randomized consumption; tolerance in genetically susceptible people rests on a non-significant caffeine effect (P>0.1) in 35 medium/high TT carriers, whose caffeine–placebo difference (about 0.4 points by the editors' reading of Figure 4) is about the size of the significant difference in non-/low consumers with CC or CT; no test of caffeine groups against nonconsumers on placebo is reported for the no-net-benefit claim, and in Figure 1 the medium group on caffeine sits slightly above that benchmark; the abstract's headache on placebo in medium/high consumers holds for high consumers only (p. 1979); and the TT anxiety effect is significant in one of three specifications (session 1 with baseline covariate, P=0.002; without it, P=0.067; combined model, P=0.008, above the corrected threshold). The authors discuss but do not test the alternative that frequent consumers are constitutionally less alert (p. 1980).

timeline.event: Goldstein et al.: coffee drinkers and abstainers given caffeine; cited here as showing a similar alertness pattern (p. 1979)
Evans & Griffiths: caffeine consumers chronically withdrawn from caffeine became anxious after a caffeine challenge, those maintained on 900 mg a day did not (as described, p. 1979)
Alsene et al.: rs5751876 TT carriers became more anxious after 150 mg (not after 50 or 450 mg) in infrequent consumers (as described, pp. 1974, 1979)

James & Rogers: withdrawal-reversal hypothesis, the secondary objective tested here (p. 1974); Haskell et al.: alertness benefits in self-described nonconsumers, whose pretreatment salivary caffeine (0.36 µg/ml) the authors contrast with this study's 0.014–0.024 µg/ml (p. 1980)

Cornelis et al.: in 2,735 Hispanic Americans (survivors of a first myocardial infarction and controls), TT carriers were less likely to take more than 200 mg a day, which disagrees with this study's habitual-intake result (as described, pp. 1981–1982)
Childs et al.: rs5751876, rs2298383 and rs4822492, but not rs3761422, predicted caffeine-induced anxiety (as described, p. 1979)
Rogers et al.: report from the same protocol and test day (performance and alertness, 369 participants); not independent of this paper

replication.where_it_stands: The association of the ADORA2A rs5751876 TT genotype with greater anxiety after caffeine agrees in direction with two earlier, smaller studies of infrequent consumers (Alsene et al., 2003; Childs et al., 2008, as described here), but here it depends on the analysis chosen. Whether this genotype lowers habitual intake is disputed: this study found no such effect and Cornelis et al. (2007) found one. Tolerance to caffeine-induced anxiety and the withdrawal-reversal account of alertness rest on comparisons of self-selected consumer groups; the companion card (sc_rogers_2013) records that other groups found no consumer-group differences. This paper and Rogers et al. (2013) share participants, test day and rating scales and must be counted as one study.
