what_would_settle_it: Randomizing habitual consumption rather than observing it: regular caffeine consumers randomized to long-term abstinence or continued intake, then given blinded caffeine and placebo challenges, with genotype recorded, would separate tolerance and withdrawal from self-selection; a preregistered comparison of caffeine-treated regular consumers with nonconsumers on placebo would test the no-net-benefit claim directly.

domains.domain: Randomization process
domains.note: Stratified randomization by interview-reported intake and age is stated (p. 1974), but sequence generation and allocation concealment are not described, the numbers allocated to caffeine and placebo are never reported, and baseline values by arm are not shown; the analysis groups were defined afterwards from a questionnaire, so balance within them is not guaranteed by the stratification.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Identical capsules, double-blind, taken in the laboratory at the scheduled times (Table 1 and Drug Administration, p. 1975).

domains.domain: Bias due to missing outcome data
domains.note: 13 of 416 lost after the first capsule (8 withdrawals, 5 equipment failures; p. 1976); all 5 withdrawals among medium/high consumers were on placebo, mostly for headache or sickness, so missingness probably depends on the outcome and makes the medium/high placebo group look better than it was. The 20 saliva exclusions used a pre-treatment sample.

domains.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Self-ratings by participants blind to treatment, computer-administered. Knowing they had abstained may colour consumer-group comparisons, not the caffeine–placebo contrast.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No registration; several analyses reported as data not shown; the genotype effect is presented from the one specification that reached significance (session 1 with baseline covariate); other outcomes deferred to later papers.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: RoB 2 applies to the randomized caffeine-versus-placebo contrast, which is well blinded; some concerns arise from unreported randomization details and arm sizes, outcome-related withdrawals and analysis-dependent genotype results. The comparisons between consumer groups, which carry the tolerance, withdrawal and no-net-benefit conclusions, are not randomized and by ROBINS-E standards would be at high risk of bias from confounding (self-selection, adjusted only for age, gender and smoking). The genotype analyses are a candidate-gene association in 379 people (95% white European; results held in the 361 of European descent). It may be cited for the acute effects of 100 mg plus 150 mg of caffeine on self-rated anxiety, alertness and headache within each consumer group after about 16 h without caffeine, and for the pattern across self-selected groups; for tolerance and withdrawal reversal only as the authors' interpretation; and for the TT-anxiety association as a replication whose significance depends on the analysis.

key_findings.finding: 416 people (218 women, 198 men) were randomized to caffeine or placebo, and 379 were analysed (162 non-/low and 217 medium/high consumers). Removed: 4 without genetic data, 15 non-/low consumers whose baseline saliva had caffeine and/or paraxanthine above 0.2 µg/ml, 5 medium/high consumers with baseline salivary caffeine above 2 µg/ml, 8 who withdrew after at least the first capsule, and 5 with data lost to equipment malfunction.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 1973); Methods › Participants and Randomization, 1st paragraph (p. 1974); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 1976)
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: 416 − 4 − 15 − 5 − 8 − 5 = 379. The saliva sample was taken at 11:10, before the first capsule at 11:15 (Table 1, p. 1975).

key_findings.finding: All five medium/high consumers who withdrew had been given placebo (four gave headache and feeling sick as the reason, one gave none); of the three non-/low consumers who withdrew, two had caffeine and one placebo. The 33 removed for saliva, withdrawal or missing data did not differ in rs5751876 genotype from the 379 analysed (chi-squared 0.05, df 2).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The analysed medium/high placebo group therefore lacks the people most affected by abstinence; its headache and alertness deficits are, if anything, underestimated.

key_findings.finding: Randomization to caffeine or placebo was stratified by habitual intake (under 40 vs at least 40 mg/day) and age (under 30 vs at least 30 years) as reported at the recruitment interview; the consumer groups used in the analysis were assigned afterwards from an intake questionnaire completed in the week before testing and analysed after the participant had been tested. Sequence generation, allocation concealment and the numbers given caffeine and placebo are not reported.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Participants and Randomization, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: 44% of participants came from respondents to a postal survey, selected at random within strata of intake and age to obtain similar numbers of infrequent and frequent consumers, although only 10% of that population took under 40 mg/day; the rest were recruited by advertisement and word of mouth. Inclusion required age 18 to 65, good health, willingness to take caffeine and give blood, at most light smoking and normal blood pressure.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Participants and Randomization, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The four consumer groups (N 81, L 81, M 109, H 108) had mean habitual intakes of 1.3, 19, 128 and 346 mg/day and mean ages of 34.1, 29.9, 32.5 and 35.4 years (F(3, 375)=3.23, P=0.023); 47% were men, 16.5% smokers and 95% white European. The authors say smokers tended to be over-represented in the higher-intake groups (7, 13, 22 and 20 smokers; chi-squared 4.99, df 3, P>0.1, Table 2). Intake ranged from 0 mg (43 participants) to 778 mg/day, with 55 above 300 mg/day.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph, and Participant Characteristics (p. 1976); Table 2 and the paragraph below it (p. 1977)

key_findings.finding: Baseline salivary caffeine was 0.014, 0.024, 0.18 and 0.39 µg/ml in the N, L, M and H groups; in those given caffeine it was 1.64 µg/ml 90 min after the first dose and 2.86 µg/ml 90 min after the second.
key_findings.locator: Systemic Caffeine Concentrations

key_findings.finding: Before any capsule, higher habitual intake went with more anxiety (F(3, 370)=2.66, P=0.048), lower alertness (F(3, 365)=5.74, P=0.001, smoking as covariate) and more headache (F(3, 370)=5.05, P=0.002).
key_findings.locator: Consumer Status by Caffeine Effects, 3rd paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Caffeine's effect depended on consumer group for all three ratings (caffeine by consumer status: anxiety F(3, 362)=7.03, P=0.0001; alertness F(3, 362)=6.06, P=0.0005; headache F(3, 362)=9.52, P<0.0001); adding smoking as a covariate left the alertness interaction essentially unchanged (F(3, 357)=6.31, P=0.0004). No effect involved dose or session, so the figures pool the post-treatment sessions.
key_findings.locator: Consumer Status by Caffeine Effects, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Caffeine increased anxiety in the N and L groups (P<0.01 each) but not in the M or H groups. Editors' reading of Figure 1 (approximate, 0–8 scale), caffeine vs placebo: about 1.2 vs 0.5 (N), 1.4 vs 0.7 (L), 0.9 vs 0.8 (M) and 0.8 vs 1.0 (H).
key_findings.locator: Consumer Status by Caffeine Effects, 2nd paragraph (p. 1977); Figure 1, top panel (p. 1978)
key_findings.note: Values read from a 300-dpi crop of Figure 1; they are not printed in the text.

key_findings.finding: Among those given placebo, alertness fell with increasing habitual intake; caffeine raised alertness in the M and H groups (P<0.01 each) but not in N or L. The authors state that caffeine raised no group above the alertness of nonconsumers on placebo; no test of that comparison is reported. Editors' reading of Figure 1 (approximate): placebo about 4.9 (N), 4.7 (L), 4.4 (M) and 3.7 (H); caffeine about 4.8, 5.0, 5.1 and 4.9.
key_findings.locator: Consumer Status by Caffeine Effects, 2nd paragraph (p. 1977); Figure 1, middle panel (p. 1978)

key_findings.finding: Headache was higher on placebo than on caffeine in the H group (P<0.01) and higher on caffeine than on placebo in the nonconsumer group (P<0.05), as marked in Figure 1 and stated in the Discussion; the Results text names the low group instead (see reporting issues). Editors' reading of Figure 1 (approximate): H about 1.8 on placebo vs 0.9 on caffeine; N about 1.2 on caffeine vs 0.7 on placebo; M about 1.1 in both.
key_findings.locator: Consumer Status by Caffeine Effects, 2nd paragraph (p. 1977); Figure 1, bottom panel (p. 1978); Discussion, 5th paragraph (p. 1980)

key_findings.finding: ADORA2A rs5751876 and anxiety after the first 100 mg dose: caffeine F(1, 366)=8.97, P=0.003; genotype F(2, 366)=7.12, P=0.0009; caffeine by genotype F(2, 366)=2.72, P=0.067. With baseline anxiety as covariate the caffeine by genotype interaction was F(2, 365)=6.57, P=0.002, below the corrected threshold of 0.00625; caffeine raised anxiety in TT carriers (P<0.01) but not in CC or CT carriers, by 0.67 points in TT against 0.11 in CC and CT combined (0–8 scale).
key_findings.locator: Genotype Distributions and Genotype by Caffeine Effects, 3rd paragraph (p. 1977); Table 3 (p. 1979); Figure 3 (p. 1980); Discussion, 7th paragraph (p. 1981)

key_findings.finding: Of the other SNPs, only rs3761422, almost completely linked with rs5751876 (D′=1, R²=0.92), gave similar results (TT on caffeine 1.65 ± 0.15 vs placebo 0.95 ± 0.17, P<0.01); rs2298383 (P=0.018) did not pass the corrected threshold; no ADORA1 SNP was associated with caffeine-induced anxiety (P>0.1) and no SNP with caffeine's effects on alertness or headache (P>0.05; data not shown). Two ADORA1 SNPs were excluded for departing from Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium (P=0.029 and 0.023).
key_findings.locator: Genotype Distributions and Genotype by Caffeine Effects, 1st paragraph (p. 1977), 3rd paragraph (continued in the left column of p. 1978) and 5th paragraph (p. 1978, right column); Table 3 (p. 1979)

key_findings.finding: In the model combining consumer group (non-/low vs medium/high), rs5751876 genotype (CC and CT vs TT), caffeine and session, with baseline anxiety as covariate: caffeine F(1, 361)=28.36, P<0.0001; caffeine by consumer status F(1, 361)=7.00, P=0.009; genotype F(1, 361)=6.44, P=0.012 and caffeine by genotype F(1, 361)=7.16, P=0.008, neither below the corrected threshold of 0.00625; consumer status by genotype by caffeine F<1. In planned comparisons caffeine raised anxiety in non-/low consumers with TT (P<0.05) and with CC or CT (P<0.01); in medium/high consumers with TT the rise was not significant (P>0.1), in what the authors call a relatively small sample.
key_findings.locator: Consumer Status by ADORA2A Genotype by Caffeine Effects: Anxiety, 1st paragraph (p. 1978); Figure 4 (p. 1981)
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of Figure 4 (approximate, 0–8 scale): TT, non-/low consumers about 1.76 on caffeine vs 0.84 on placebo; TT, medium/high about 1.37 vs 1.00; CC and CT, non-/low about 1.10 vs 0.74; CC and CT, medium/high about 0.85 vs 0.79. The medium/high TT difference (about 0.4) is about the size of the significant non-/low CC and CT difference (about 0.35). Medium/high TT carriers numbered 35 (p. 1978); their split by treatment is not reported.

key_findings.finding: rs5751876 genotype did not differ between non-/low (CC 62, CT 70, TT 30) and medium/high consumers (CC 84, CT 98, TT 35) (chi-squared 0.39, df 2, P=0.82). Among medium/high consumers, TT carriers took more caffeine from coffee (F(1, 212)=5.91, P=0.016, corrected threshold 0.017), somewhat less from tea (P=0.09) and no different total (P>0.1); for rs3761422, caffeine from coffee was 181 ± 24 mg/day in TT against 106 ± 10 in CC and CT (F(1, 212)=8.03, P=0.005).
key_findings.locator: ADORA2A Genotype and Habitual Caffeine Consumption (p. 1978, right column, continuing on p. 1979); Figure 5 (p. 1981)

key_findings.finding: The genotype effects remained significant when the analysis was limited to participants of European descent (n=361).
key_findings.locator: Genotype Distributions and Genotype by Caffeine Effects, 4th paragraph (p. 1978, right column, top)

key_findings.finding: The authors read the H group's lower alertness and more headache on placebo, after less than 24 h without caffeine (habitual intake 346 mg/day), as withdrawal effects; the M group showed only lower alertness.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Against under-recruitment of anxiety-prone people, the authors report TT frequencies close to Hardy–Weinberg expectations in both consumer groups (observed 30 and 35, expected 26 and 33) and that fewer than 2% of contacted infrequent consumers who did not take part cited concern about caffeine's adverse effects.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 10th paragraph (left column)

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say headache was increased by caffeine in the low (L) group (p. 1977), but Figure 1 marks the significant caffeine–placebo difference (P<0.05) at the nonconsumer (N) point (p. 1978), and the Discussion attributes the increase to the N group (p. 1980).
reporting_issues.consequence: Going by the figure and the Discussion, the headache increase on caffeine was in nonconsumers; a claim citing the Results text would name the wrong group.

reporting_issues.issue: The numbers allocated to caffeine and placebo are not reported in the article (online supplement not read), overall or within consumer or genotype groups; Table 2 describes consumer groups only, and sequence generation and allocation concealment are not described (416 randomized, 379 analysed).
reporting_issues.consequence: Balance between arms, and the size of the small subgroups behind the genotype-by-consumer comparisons, cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: Randomization was stratified on intake reported at the recruitment interview, but the analysis groups (under 40 vs at least 40 mg/day) were assigned from a questionnaire analysed after testing; how many participants changed category is not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Stratification may not have balanced the arms within the analysis groups; the extent is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says placebo in medium/high participants increased headache (p. 1973), but Figure 1 shows the headache difference in the H group only (p. 1978), and the Discussion says the M group showed only lower alertness (p. 1979).
reporting_issues.consequence: Headache after overnight abstinence is supported for the high-intake group (mean 346 mg/day), not for medium consumers.

reporting_issues.issue: The legend of Figure 5 does not say that it shows medium/high consumers only, which the text indicates (F(1, 212) for the medium/high group, p. 1978).
reporting_issues.consequence: Read alone, Figure 5 could be taken to describe the whole sample.

reporting_issues.issue: Rogers et al. (2013), from the same protocol and test day, analysed 369 participants (157 non-/low, 212 medium/high): those with salivary confirmation of consumer status and abstinence and complete data for mental alertness, sleepiness, anxiety/jitteriness and task performance (Rogers et al., 2013, pp. 229, 231, 233); this paper analyses 379 (p. 1976). Neither report itemizes the 10 people (5 in each consumer group) in this paper's set but not in the 2013 set, so the two analysis sets cannot be reconciled person by person.
reporting_issues.consequence: The two reports' analysis sets differ by 10 people, 5 in each consumer group; neither can be checked against the other's exclusions from this paper.
